Online university or other equivalent platform to support
university-level science, technology, engineering and
mathematics education in the least developed countries
Report of the Secretary-General*
Summary
The present report is submitted pursuant to General Assembly resolution 76/258,
by which the Assembly endorsed the Doha Programme of Action for the Least
Developed Countries, as contained in the annex to that resolution. In the Programme
of Action, Member States committed to undertaking feasibility studies to explore the
possibility of establishing an online university or other equivalent platforms to
support online graduate and postgraduate university-level science, technology,
engineering and mathematics education in least developed countries and recently
graduated countries. In that regard, they requested the Secretary-General to submit a
report outlining, inter alia, the mapping of existing initiatives, possible new
modalities, resource requirements, accreditation and sustainable funding sources.
* The present report was submitted to the conference services for processing after the deadline
for technical reasons beyond the control of the submitting office.

I. Introduction

1. In the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries, which the
General Assembly endorsed by its resolution 76/258, Member States committed to
undertaking feasibility studies to explore the possibility of establishing an online
university or other equivalent platforms to support online graduate and postgraduate
university-level science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in least
developed countries and recently graduated countries with a view to, inter alia,
providing policy support to promote distance education and open learning for
graduate and postgraduate studies in science, technology, engineering and
mathematics, ensuring a 50/50 gender balance at all levels while guaranteeing special
access for the poorest and people in vulnerable situations; creating a virtual network
of educational institutions within and beyond least developed countries; assist ing in
course design and curriculum development; and leading to scale and sustainability of
the education system, taking into account all pre-existing initiatives developed by the
relevant partners in a comprehensive manner.

2. In addition, Member States requested the Secretary-General to submit a report,
outlining, inter alia, the mapping of existing initiatives, possible new modalities,
resource requirements, accreditation and sustainable funding sources for an online
university or other equivalent platforms, to the General Assembly for its consideration.

3. With a view to fulfilling that mandate, in 2024, the Office of the High
Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries
and Small Island Developing States conducted a desk review of the broader higher
education landscape. Following the desk review, the Office of the High
Representative organized a high-level expert group meeting on the feasibility of
establishing an online university for the least developed countries from 3 to 4 June
2025.1 The present report was prepared on the basis of the findings of the desk review,
the consultations that the Office held with relevant agencies and entities within the
United Nations system and the outcomes of the high-level expert group meeting. In
the present report, it is emphasized that establishing an online university for least
developed countries is feasible and that such a university is needed in order to enhance
access to quality higher education opportunities for the rapidly growing youth
populations of such countries.

4. The proposed online university or equivalent platform is not envisioned as a
degree-issuing institution. Instead, its purpose would be to build the capacity of
existing institutions in least developed countries to promote graduate and
postgraduate science, technology, engineering and mathematics educational
initiatives, with an emphasis on expanding access to high -quality learning
opportunities for the poorest and marginalized populations, as envisioned in the Doha
Programme of Action.

5. Despite the emergence of numerous initiatives to support online learning in
higher education institutions in developing countries, only a few operate at scale or
reach women, Indigenous groups, marginalized communities and persons with
disabilities. Desk reviews have revealed a glaring gap in online education in least
developed countries, with only a handful of institutions offering online science,
technology, engineering and mathematics education through digital platforms. In the
few cases where institutions offer online programmes, they typically rely on a blended
model that incorporates some in-person instruction or requires students to go to
community learning centres in order to access to the Internet, technology and faculty.

Fully online science, technology, engineering and mathematics education remains
virtually non-existent in these countries. These hybrid models reflect ongoing efforts
to overcome systemic barriers to access and quality in higher education, but they are
isolated examples. Enhanced international cooperation, targeted investment and
institutional capacity-building will be essential to advancing inclusive and equitable
science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in line with the Doha
Programme of Action and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

6. In view of the persistent and widening gaps in access to higher education in least
developed countries, an online university or equivalent platform would offer innovative
solutions by deploying cost-effective digital technologies, building strategic
partnerships and promoting robust investments to overcome access, geographical and
institutional barriers. It would collaborate with existing higher education institutions in
least developed countries and foster partnerships with a range of stakeholders to de liver
targeted capacity-building, scalable solutions and pathways towards global recognition
of science, technology, engineering and mathematics qualifications earned in least
developed countries. It holds significant promise as a platform to catalyse efforts aimed
at meeting the urgent and growing demand for higher education and unlocking
opportunities where they are needed the most.

7. Relevant United Nations system organizations, in particular, the International
Telecommunications Union (ITU), United Nations Educational, Scientific and
Cultural Organization (UNESCO), United Nations Technology Bank for the Least
Developed Countries and United Nations University (UNU), are well placed to
provide strategic and technical guidance and support to such an endeavour.

8. In the present report, the Secretary-General examines the current landscape of
science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in least developed
countries, highlighting critical gaps in access, quality and delivery. He analyses the
underlying challenges and the proposed preliminary solutions aimed at addressing
those barriers. In addition, the Secretary-General outlines proposals for advancing the
establishment of the proposed online university or equivalent platform and, in that
regard, recommends that the Office of the High Representative undertake further
consultations in order to define a proposed structure and address governance, resource
requirements and other institutional matters.

II. Overview of higher education and science, technology,
engineering and mathematics capacity gaps in least
developed countries

9. The least developed countries, which currently number 45, are home to
approximately 14 per cent of the global population. In total, 31.4 per cent of the
population of the least developed countries live in extreme poverty. Those countries
account for only 1.3 per cent of global gross domestic product (GDP), 1.4 per cent of
global foreign direct investment and under 1 per cent of global merchandising exports. 2

10. Under Sustainable Development Goal 4, ensuring inclusive and equitable
quality education and promoting lifelong opportunities for all involves providing
education at all levels, from early childhood education to tertiary education,
equipping individuals with the skills needed for employment and active participation
in society. The working-age (15–64 years) population in least developed countries is
expected to double from 610 million in 2020 to 1.2 billion in 2050. This rapid growth
makes investing in tertiary education a priority.

11. The higher education landscape in the least developed countries is evolving and
currently undergoing rapid transformation. There is increasing recognition in those
countries of the role of higher education in sustainable development. Despite the huge
potential and urgency of promoting higher education, least developed countries face
major challenges in respect of both increasing access to and improving the quality of
higher education. They are in a vicious cycle of low income and low educational
opportunities and attainment that results in lack of decent and productive
employment. Higher education systems across all least developed countries are
characterized by low enrolment rates, limited institutional capacity and significant
disparities in access and quality.

A. Low enrolment rates in tertiary education

12. Despite notable efforts to make tertiary education more available in least
developed countries, the gap in the gross tertiary education enrolment rate between
those countries and the rest of the world has continued to grow. The data indicate that,
from 2019 to 2023, the gross tertiary education enrolment rate in least developed
countries had stagnated at 11.2 per cent, compared with the global average of 43.3 per
cent in 2023 (see figure I).
Figure I
Tertiary education enrolment rate

13. The global higher education gross enrolment ratio masks large disparities
between regions of the world. The higher education gross enrolment rat e is highest in
Europe and North America, at 75 per cent, and lowest in sub -Saharan Africa, at 8 per
cent. 3 There are also wide disparities in enrolment across and within countries,
between rural and urban areas and across different segments of the population. For
example, in 2023, in sub-Saharan Africa, 78 women were enrolled in higher education
for every 100 men, whereas the global ratio was 113 women for every 100 men.4

14. In the least developed countries, there are approximately 1,530 universities (577
public and 953 private) recognized by the International Association of Universities.
That figure accounts for just 7.1 per cent of the 21,580 universities worldwide,
highlighting the scarcity of higher education institutions in least developed countries.
Moreover, the data reveal a striking disparity in higher education infrastructure
between least developed countries and other regions of the world. As at 2025, least
developed countries have an average of only 0.61 universities per 100,000 young
persons aged 15–29, far below the levels in Europe (4.07), North America (3.20) and
Latin America and the Caribbean (2.37) (see figure II). Although certain countries,
such as Haiti and Timor-Leste, stand out with relatively better access, the majority,
such as Ethiopia (0.18), Bangladesh (0.25) and the United Republic of Tanzania
(0.24), are well below the global average. It should be noted that those figures reflect
the number of institutions, not their capacity or quality.
Figure II
Number of universities per 100,000 population aged 15–29 years, 2025
Source: International Association of Universities, World Higher Education Database (2025).

15. Several interconnected factors, including socioeconomic, structural and cultural
challenges, contribute to the low enrolment rate in the least developed countries. In
many cases, institutions of higher learning are geographically concentrated in urban
centres, limiting the availability of educational services to populations residing in
remote and rural areas. This structural imbalance is further compounded by a scarcity
of available enrolment spaces, particularly in public universities. Notwithstanding
persistent challenges related to financing and infrastructure, public institutions in
least developed countries continue to accommodate most tertiary -level students,
reflecting their central role in national education systems.

16. In recent decades, the number of private universities in least developed countries
has grown significantly and now exceeds that of public institutions. While private
universities play an important role in absorbing demand and alleviating pressure on
overstretched public systems, their predominantly tuition-based models often
reinforce existing structural inequities in access to higher education. As a result,
students from lower-income backgrounds remain disproportionately excluded from
opportunities for tertiary education, deepening socioeconomic disparities in least
developed countries.

17. Low educational attainment at the secondary level continues to pose a major
impediment to increasing enrolment in tertiary education in least developed countries.
This challenge is especially acute among marginalized and displaced groups and
lower-income segments of the population, which face compounded barriers to

progression within the education system. As a result, tertiary education enrolment
rates in least developed countries continue to lag, constraining the development of a

B. Capacity constraint and quality assurance challenges

18. Owing to the limited number of higher education institutions that are available
and accessible, capacity constraints manifest in overcrowded institutions, inadequate
infrastructure and a shortage of qualified faculty. These structural limitations not only
restrict opportunities for higher education, they also undermine the overall resilience
and responsiveness of least developed countries’ higher education systems with
regard to meeting the demands of an increasingly dynamic and knowledge -driven
global economy.

19. The capacity challenge extends to the scope of graduate and postgraduate
courses available in least developed countries. While enrolment in tertiary education
institutions offering science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees has
increased, 95.4 per cent of courses in those subjects are being offered in non -least
developed countries and only 4.6 per cent in least developed countries, although
latter’s share of the global youth population is 18.6 per cent. 5 This disparity (see
figure III) highlights the urgent need to expand science, technology, engineering and
mathematics education opportunities in least developed countries, in order to support
inclusive development and global workforce readiness.

20. Higher education, especially in science, technology, engineering and
mathematics, is crucial for least developed countries to drive socioeconomic
development and achieve parity with more advanced countries. The least developed
countries, however, are falling behind in this area. Gender disparities in science,
technology, engineering and mathematics are pronounced. Globally, only 35 per cent
of graduates in those fields are women because of the barriers posed by overall lower

to technology. Specific data for women in least developed countries are unavailable.

21. Rapid and often unregulated expansion of higher education institutions has led
to overcrowded classrooms, overburdened faculty, declining investment in such
critical infrastructure as laboratories and libraries, shrinking academic activities and
the deterioration of facilities.6 These conditions have contributed to an erosion in the
quality of higher education in many least developed countries.

22. Both internal and external quality assurance are needed and play an important
role in assuring stakeholders that acceptable educational standards are being
maintained and enhanced. Despite the launch of several African regional frameworks
to promote harmonization of quality assurance and accreditation in higher education,
quality assurance in least developed countries remain fragmented owing to a lack of
robust national mechanisms, lack of coordination between ministries, universities and
regulatory agencies and limited participation in international peer reviews and
benchmarking exercises.

23. According to UNESCO, developed countries have significantly more national
quality assurance institutions and national qualification frameworks than most
developing countries. Of the approximately 800 higher education quality assurance
bodies operating worldwide, only 170 have undergone external evaluation, among which
very few are from the least developed countries. 7 Strengthening quality assurance in
least developed countries will require capacity-building, strengthening regional
collaboration and alignment with global standards, such as those promoted by UNESCO.

24. The Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher
Education is the first international treaty on the recognition of higher education
qualifications. The Convention, which is aimed at streamlining and standardizing the
evaluation and acceptance of academic credentials worldwide, could be the impetus
needed for countries, including the least developed countries, to embrace a
standardized recognition system.

C. Digital divide

25. The digital divide is a major structural barrier that further exacerbates the higher
education gaps in least developed countries. According to the International
Telecommunications Union (ITU), the digital connectivity gap between least developed
countries and the rest of the world has widened.8 In 2024, only 35 per cent of people
in those countries were online, compared with 68 per cent globally and 93 per cent in
high-income countries. Although two thirds of the overall population of the least
developed countries is offline, ITU data show, that in 2023, 45 per cent of young
persons aged 15–24 in those countries were already online, giving an online learning
platform an immediate, sizeable audience while still leaving room for outreach and
expansion as connectivity grows. 9 Significant disparities persist between men and
women and between rural and urban areas. Only 83 per cent of people in least developed
countries are covered by a mobile broadband signal (3G or higher), compared with
95 per cent globally. High Internet costs remain a major barrier, with access in least

developed countries costing about four times the global average.10 The lack of access
to electricity remains an obstacle in least developed countries attempting to adopt online
learning. In 2023, 59 per cent of the population in those countries had access to
electricity.11 The challenges relating to the use of online learning in those countries
became particularly apparent during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic.
Data from World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) studies confirm that
learning losses were larger in countries with lower GDP per capita.12,13 While most
high-income countries were able to quickly roll out remote teaching and learning, the
least developed countries struggled to respond, suspending classes and examinations
for an extended period, more than a year in many instances.

26. While considerable efforts are under way in several least developed countries to
bridge the digital divide in higher education, including by strengthening public -
private partnerships to invest in the digital infrastructure, such as broadband service
and Internet access, bridging the digital divide, in particular in rural areas, where
60 per cent of the least developed country populations live, will require sustained
investment and time.14 Given the urgency of ensuring inclusive and equitable access
to learning opportunities, interim strategies must be actively pursued, including the
deployment of offline learning tools, the adaptation of digital platforms for low -
bandwidth environments and the creation of public access hubs to support
community-based learning, with a view to providing crucial tools to ensure progress
in education inclusion.

D. Financing

27. The low level of investment in higher education in least developed countries is
a key factor contributing to both the limited availability and the broader quality
challenges of tertiary education. In total, least developed countries spen t
approximately $51 billion on education in 2024, representing 3.2 per cent of their
GDP, compared with $4.2 trillion globally, which accounts for 3.8 per cent of global
GDP. Specifically, for tertiary education, least developed countries allocate d 20.3 per
cent of their government education expenditure, amounting to just $10.4 billion, while
global spending on tertiary education is estimated at $908.4 billion. 15 Globally,
spending on tertiary education amounts to 1.1 per cent of government expenditure in
the least developed countries, although those countries account for 14 per cent of the
global population and 18.8 per cent of the global youth population. Those figures
underscore the limited financial resources available for education in least developed
countries, in particular for higher education, which affects the quality, accessibility
and capacity of the education systems in those countries.

28. Total education aid at the global level reached a record high of $16.6 billion in
2022. The proportion of official development assistance (ODA) directed towards
education, however, declined from 9.3 per cent in 2019 to 7.6 per cent in 2022. 16 Of
the total ODA received, the largest portion was directed towards basic education

29. Only 30 per cent of education aid provided by the 10 largest donors to sub-Saharan
Africa was disbursed directly to recipient countries. The remaining 70 per cent was
channelled through donor aid agencies, international and domestic non-governmental
organizations and multilateral organizations.19 This indirect allocation often results in
fragmentation and lack of government leadership, underscoring the need for adequate,
efficient and equitable investment in education, especially in countries with great gaps.
In addition, students from least developed countries are almost twice as likely t o pursue
tertiary education abroad compared with their peers from other countries. Consequently,
they are more likely to take skilled jobs overseas, increasing the risk of brain drain .

30. Public spending on education is highly unequal within countries globally, with
the top income quintiles capturing a disproportionate share of available resources. In
a 2024 report, the World Bank and UNESCO noted that inequalities tend to be highest
in poorer countries, such as the least developed countries, where differences in
enrolment patterns by income quintile is most unequal for tertiary education, as those
with access to this level of education mainly come from wealthier households. As a
result, wealthier households receive a much higher share of public expenditure for
higher education compared with poorer households. The World Bank and UNESCO
also found that funding for secondary and tertiary education becomes more equitable
as enrolment increases at the primary and secondary levels among the poor.20

III. Global overview of online and open learning initiatives and
their efficacy

31. While the terms open university and online university are often used
interchangeably, they denote distinct models within the higher education landscape.
Open universities are primarily defined by their commitment to open access and
characterized by minimal entry requirements, lack of age restrictions and inclusive
policies aimed at democratizing education for non-traditional learners, including
working adults, individuals in remote or rural areas and marginalized populations. A
principal point of differentiation lies in their respective modes of delivery. Online
universities focus predominantly on digital platforms, offering education primarily
through virtual means with structured online curricula. By contrast, open universities
frequently employ a broader range of instructional modalities, including printed
materials, radio and television broadcasts and localized learning support centres,
enabling flexible and multichannel access to education.

32. Open and distance learning has become a central global strategy to broaden
access to education, in particular in developing countries. In recent years, the
increasing demand for higher education coupled with greater access to the Internet

has led to the introduction of distance blended and online learning as new ways of

33. A key component of this changing educational landscape is the development of
open educational resources, which may include digital resources, such as e-textbooks,
and videos and virtual labs that are licenced for free educational use and easily
accessible online. Open educational resources are digital public goods available on
an open copyright licence that respects the intellectual property rights of the copyright
owner and allow users to re-use, repurpose, adapt and redistribute such resources.
Open solutions that use open educational resources are crucial to supporting the
achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

34. Massive online open courses are another recent development in education.
Between 2011 and 2021, the number of learners reached by such courses increased from
300,000 to 220 million around the world, excluding China. 21 In 2021, a total of
40 million new learners signed up for at least one massive online open course. No prior
qualifications are required to enrol in massive online open courses. Such course s,
however, are not necessarily open educational resources. While some of the world’s
leading universities, such as MIT and Harvard, offer massive online open courses, the
fees for the certification track can be a significant access barrier for learners fro m low-
income backgrounds in developing countries. Many of the most popular massive online
open courses cannot be reused without permission from the original provider. Massive
online open courses mainly benefit learners from richer countries owing to divides in
digital skills, Internet access, language and course design. A study of higher educa tion
repositories with open educational resource collections found that nearly 90 per cent
were created in Europe or North America and that 92 per cent of the material in the
OER Commons global library is in English, which affects who can use such content. 22

35. Developing countries and least developed countries, in particular, face a unique
set of challenges in broadening access to massive online open courses and open
educational resources. A systematic review of the research into the use of open online
learning technologies in developing countries context reveals five interrelated barriers
or challenges: (a) access to the Internet; (b) digital literacy; (c) online pedagogies;
(d) the context of content; and (e) flow of knowledge between North and South. 23

36. Offering science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees fully online
at the undergraduate or graduate level remains a challenge owing to the need for
laboratory work; there are no official data available for courses in those fields. Some
open universities have addressed that challenge by using television or video to
demonstrate lab work. Blended models of science, technology, engineering and
mathematics courses are more common, whereby students attend their laboratory
classes in person at designated facilities. More recently, digital simulations have been
developed to demonstrate scientific processes that are difficult to replicate in a
traditional laboratory, while virtual labs enable students to remotely control
laboratory equipment. The Remote Access to Laboratory Equipment initiative of
UNESCO is helping to bridge that gap by enabling scientists and students in under -
resourced regions, in particular in Africa, to gain access to and operate advanced
scientific instruments remotely, often for the first time. This initiative not only
facilitates remote experimentation but also provides structured training and technical
support, thereby building sustainable local capacity and empowering researchers to
conduct high-quality science from their home institutions. While digital simulations

37. In recent years, there have been major developments in the use of artificial
intelligence in education. While artificial intelligence systems are evolving rapidly,
often outpacing regulation and sometimes without adequate safeguards or quality
assurance, their educational application could offer substantial benefits. Artificial
intelligence-driven solutions have demonstrated substantial benefits, in particular in
the following areas:
(a) Accelerated development of undergraduate curricula, in particular in
science, technology, engineering and mathematics education, through data -informed
instructional design;
(b) Adaptive learning platforms that deliver personalized educational content
based on individual learning styles and progress;
(c) Real-time feedback and continuous academic support tailored to meet the
unique needs of individual learners;
(d) Streamlined and automated student assessments, enhancing efficiency and
consistency in evaluation;
(e) Personalized career guidance, helping students make informed decisions
based on their strengths, interests and employment trends.

38. The appropriate use of artificial intelligence in online education offers significant
potential for cost savings in course design and delivery, while also enhancing the
learning experience. The quality of online learning can vary widely, however, as in th e
case of traditional classroom teaching. More than 30 years of experience in online
education has led to the emergence of a set of best practices emphasizing the importance
of clear course structure, defined weekly learning objectives, manageable study
workloads, active engagement, assignment deadlines and regular feedback.
Collaborative learning among students has also been shown to improve outcomes.

39. Integrating artificial intelligence into teaching and learning will make it possible
not only to leverage artificial intelligence to improve the design and delivery of online
courses, but also to develop explicit instructions on the responsible and effecti ve use
of artificial intelligence tools, thereby reducing the cost of design and delivery of
online courses as well. Training educators to effectively use artificial intelligence
tools can enhance instructional design, automate assessments and deliver personalized
feedback. At the same time, equipping students with digital literacy skills prepares them
to engage with artificial intelligence-powered tools and intelligent tutoring systems
using real-time application of artificial intelligence to support the delivery of
individualized learning pathways, thereby enabling both educators and learners to
become not only beneficiaries of education that is enhanced by the use of artificial
intelligence, but also informed participants in shaping its future.

IV. Input from the high-level expert group meeting

40. In addition to conducting a desk review of online education and holding bilateral
consultations, the Office of the High Representative organized a high-level expert group
meeting at United Nations Headquarters in New York on 3 and 4 June 2025. The meeting
brought together 24 distinguished global experts, including several from least developed
countries, with expertise in online and higher education, artificial intelligence, digital
transformation, policy and science, technology, engineering and mathematics curriculum
development. Participants represented the United Nations system, least developed
country Governments, academia, philanthropic foundations and the private sector. The

meeting, which was organized in close collaboration with UNESCO and UNU, benefited
from the active participation and strong support of Member States, including the
Permanent Representatives of Bangladesh, the Gambia, Malawi, Nepal, Timor-Leste,
Türkiye and Tuvalu, as well as a representative of Qatar.24 The closing session was open
to all Member States and drew significant attention and engagement.

41. Pursuant to the mandate set out in the Doha Programme of Action, the meeting
was held in order to guide the development of feasibility studies for the establishment
of an online university or equivalent platform. The programme of the meeting was
structured around five core thematic areas identified as essential to the effective
conceptualization of the proposed initiative: (a) mapping of existing initiatives;
(b) possible new modalities; (c) resource requirements; (d) quality assurance and
accreditation; and (e) sustainable funding sources. One of the cross-cutting themes of
the meeting was ensuring gender balance at all levels while guaranteeing access for
the poorest and people in vulnerable situations and avoiding duplication of efforts.

A. Mapping of existing initiatives

42. In recent years, a growing number of initiatives have emerged to support the
advancement of distance and online learning in higher education institutions in
developing countries. More than 20 relevant initiatives were identified during the
preparation of the present report, reflecting an expanding landscape of innovation that
is aimed at improving access to tertiary education. Mapping efforts reveal a modest
but growing number of open and online universities operating in least developed
countries. Many of those institutions have adopted blended learning models,
combining elements of both open and online universities. They are pioneering new
approaches to distance education across a range of disciplines, in particular in teacher
training, public policy and information technology. Only a limited number of those
institutions, however, currently offer fully accredited online science, technology,
engineering and mathematics degree programmes. Those that do often rely on a mix
of instructional methods, rather than using virtual platforms specifically built to
deliver the entire course structure online, thus highlighting a persistent gap in the
provision of science, technology, engineering and mathematics education at scale in
least developed countries.

43. The two largest initiatives reviewed in terms of number of students were the
Bangladesh Open University, with has more than 1 million students, including some
outside the country, and the University of the People, which is based in the United
States of America. The latter is a fully online university with 153,000 students from
209 countries, including 35,000 students in the least developed countries. Both
institutions emphasize flexibility, affordability and accessibility, in particular for
underserved populations.

44. The African Virtual University, a pan-African intergovernmental institution, is
helping African countries to implement online learning. The African Virtual
University was established by African Governments with a mandate to significantly
increase access to quality higher education and training through the innovative use of
information and communications technology (ICT). Other areas in which the
University has been involved include designing and implementing e -learning
projects, training instructors for e-learning platforms and providing resources for
managing a digital library. It has trained 43,000 graduates and has 31 learning centres
in 17 countries, of which 14 are in least developed countries.

45. The Université numérique Cheikh Hamidou Kane, based in Senegal, offers
public online university degree courses accredited at the national and African levels
in science, technology, engineering and mathematics using an innovative model.
Accredited by the national quality assurance authority for higher education of Senegal
and recognized at the regional level by the African and Malagasy Council for Higher
Education, the Université numérique Cheikh Hamidou Kane offers a strategic model
for scalable digital higher education that can be replicated in the resource-constrained
contexts of least developed countries. In 2025, the university had an enrolment
exceeding 74,000 students, with approximately 44 per cent of its academic offerings
concentrated in science, technology, engineering and digital innovation. The
university’s master’s degree programmes include such specialized fields as big data
analysis, ICT security, artificial intelligence, robotics and advanced mathematics,
demonstrating a commitment to developing students with future-ready skills and
contributing to national and regional knowledge economies. 25

46. A few least developed countries have open universities, such as the Open
University of Liberia and the Open University of the Sudan. Both use a blended model
to deliver academic programmes in which students access digital materials, use print
materials and take part in face-to-face sessions. The reach and impact of online
tertiary education in least developed countries remain difficult to quantify owing to
limited data. Moreover, standardized indicators for online education, such as
enrolment, outcomes and completion rates, are largely unavailable for least developed
countries, hindering global comparisons and making benchmarking difficult.

47. The United Nations has a number of relevant initiatives. UNU, while primarily
mandated to promote research, offers master’s and doctoral programmes directed at the
nationals of developing countries, including least developed countries. In 2024, UNU
had 321 postgraduate students enrolled across its 13 institutes in 12 countries. Of that
number, 54 per cent from developing countries and 64 per cent were women. 26 UNU
also provides online and blended courses that have the potential to reach remote
learners. Its academic focus spans biotechnology, environment, frontier technologies,
sustainability, global health and natural resource management in Africa, among other
fields. While UNU grants postgraduate degrees in the public policy domains, none of
its partner institutions are from the least developed countries. In addition, the UNESCO
Institute for Information Technologies in Education promotes the innovative use of ICT
and serves as a facilitator and enabler for achieving Sustainable Development Goal 4
(quality education) through ICT-enabled solutions and best practices. UNESCO also
promotes the Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning
Higher Education to help countries develop their own quality assurance agencies.

48. The Commonwealth of Learning is helping its constituent States, including 14
least developed countries, and institutions to use distance learning and technologies
for expanding access to education and training. It works with ministries and higher
education institutions to increase equitable access to quality tertiary education,
promotes the rapid design, development and delivery of quality gender-responsive
open educational resources and assists in the development and implementation of
employability frameworks.

49. Several international higher education networks, such as the Pan African
University, the International Network of Higher Education in Africa, the Asian
Association of Open Universities and the International Association of Universities,
among others, support distance and online learning and promote collaboration to enhance
the quality of distance learning, including by occasionally sharing open educational
resources. None of these entities, however, provide degrees in science, technology,

50. Those initiatives help to expand online education in developing countries, in

52. Each option involves trade-offs related to scalability, contextual relevance and
institutional capacity-building in the least developed countries. Among the options
considered, a hybrid model combining options B and C emerged as the most balanced
and cost-effective pathway for the proposed online university or equivalent platform
to deliver online science, technology, engineering and mathematics education. Under
this model, local universities in least developed countries would form an
interconnected network supported by the United Nations and strengthened by
partnerships with existing regional and global networks and global academic
institutions. By anchoring delivery in the local context, this approach promotes both
relevance and resilience. It would also help foster regional cooperation and capacity-
building by offering a scalable and sustainable solution to meet the growing demand
for science, technology, engineering and mathematics education across least
developed countries.

C. Resource requirements

53. Establishing a United Nations online university or equivalent platform will
require the deployment of financial and technical resources in order to find solutions
for existing gaps in digital infrastructure and address access barriers faced by least
developed countries. The entity would need funding not only to cover its
administrative costs, but also to facilitate and support the development of digital
platforms, instructional design, virtual laboratories and offline -compatible systems;
partner with global academic experts to facilitate capacity-building of faculty in least
developed countries, blended preparatory programmes for digital literacy and study
skills; and develop multilingual course materials that are contextually relevant and
responsive to local labour markets. Artificial intelligence-powered platforms have
significant potential to deliver high-quality science, technology, engineering and
mathematics content to remote areas, bypassing infrastructure limitations. Artificial
intelligence tools can also generate major cost-savings in content adaptation,
customize learning materials and automate updates, making content accessible to a
wide range of end users. A strong focus on developing and expanding digital literacy,
especially among women, marginalized groups, instructors and policymakers, will be
essential to ensure inclusion and long-term impact in relation to science, technology,
engineering and mathematics education.

54. Lack of digital connectivity is a fundamental challenge to any online learning
initiative for least developed countries. Internet access is essential not only for
educational purposes but also for economic development. This barrier can only be
removed through coordinated action by least developed country Governments,
international agencies and telecommunications companies. Reliable and seamless
access to the Internet is a necessary prerequisite for the execution of online learning.

D. Quality assurance and accreditation

55. Currently, there is a significant variation in qualifications and accreditation
mechanisms across least developed countries. As a result, it is difficult to have
academic credentials transferred to and recognized in other countries. Online degrees,
in particular those offered across borders, are often met with considerable scepticism
by employers and local academic institutions and are not recognized at all, in many
cases. This is largely because there are no national policy frameworks in place that
make it possible to formally recognize or accredit foreign or online qualifications. In
addition, many universities in least developed countries lack the administrative and
pedagogical infrastructure necessary to support blended or online partnerships with
international education providers.

56. Moreover, the recognition of online degrees in certain science, technology,
engineering and mathematics disciplines by regulatory authorities remains a
significant challenge. Even when students complete online programmes, their
credentials are often not widely accepted by employers or government bodies.
Without formal recognition from national accreditation bodies, these qualifications
often carry limited value in local job markets. Accreditation should be viewed as a
continuum, rather than a binary process, with microcredentials serving as building
blocks leading to formal recognition.

57. To address those challenges, strategies must be developed to navigate
multi-country accreditation processes, including the adoption of global, regional and
national accreditation frameworks. An online university or equivalent platform can
play a key role in supporting efforts towards building capacity to harmonize quality
assurance checks, adhering to international standards and advancing the ratification
of Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher
Education. In collaboration with UNESCO, the online university or equivalent
platform should adopt and implement a rigorous quality assessment for all least
developed country science, technology, engineering and mathematics programmes
that receive funding or support through an online university or equivalent platform.

E. Sustainable funding sources and partnerships

58. To ensure financial resilience and sustainability, the online university or
equivalent platform should seek to diversify its funding sources to include grants and
donations. It should establish knowledge partnerships with academic institutions for
pedagogical innovation, curriculum development and quality assurance, public -
private partnerships for infrastructure, connectivity and technology solutions.
Strengthening government engagement will be critical, as national authorities must
play a central role in supporting and scaling such initiatives. To ensure equitable
access, especially for those left furthest behind, scholarship schemes and targeted
financial support should also be considered.

59. A deeper review of successful models, such as the Université numérique Cheikh
Hamidou Kane, the University of the People and Smart Education Platform of China,
reveals that they offer practical lessons in scaling access, leveraging blended delivery
and ensuring employability. Education Above All offers a comprehensive package of
support, including free access to education, digital tools, financial assistance and
tailored programmes through innovative partnerships and funding models. Those
approaches should be further explored to inform the design of online university or
equivalent platform.

60. Broad-based collaboration with United Nations entities will also be required to
leverage and build on existing capacities. Key entities, including ITU, UNESCO, the
United Nations Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries and UNU, are
well positioned to contribute to science, technology, engineering and mathematics
advancement in least developed countries and support the online university or
equivalent platform.

V. Conclusion and way forward

61. The working-age population (15–64 years) in least developed countries is
projected to double from 610 million in 2020 to 1.2 billion in 2050. This demographic
shift presents a potential opportunity to realize large, sustained demographic
dividends driven by declining dependency ratios and expanding labour forces. It is
not a certainty, however, that it will be possible to take advantage of this opportunity.

=== PDF PAGE 17 ===
A/80/426
17/1925-15631
Without access to quality education and decent employment, the potential dividend
could be lost, leading to increased inequality and social instability, instead.

62. Least developed countries possess abundant renewable energy and human
potential, but they lack the capacity to fully harness them for development.
Investment in science, technology, engineering and mathematics education is
therefore essential not only to building the foundations of a knowledge-based
economy, but also to preparing for the transformative impact of such emerging
technologies as generative artificial intelligence and big data. Higher education in
science, technology, engineering and mathematics offers the least developed countries
a unique opportunity to leapfrog traditional development models and shift directly to
service-based economies.

63. Existing online degree platforms largely fail to meet the needs of the populations
in least developed countries owing to systemic and multifaceted barriers that make
quality science, technology, engineering and mathematics education inaccessible.
Infrastructure deficits, limited institutional capacity and high costs associated with
traditional models compound the challenge. Cultural and linguistic barriers further
exclude potential learners, while gender disparities intensify exclusion, as evidenced by
the fact that only 19 per cent of women in least developed countries use the Internet.

64. The proposed online university or equivalent platform could play a pivotal role
in bridging the digital and educational divide, in particular in science, technology,
engineering and mathematics fields. It could help strengthen digital infrastructure
development, human capital formation and quality assurance systems through
international cooperation, thereby narrowing the higher education enrolment gaps in
least developed countries. By brokering strategic partnerships that may otherwise be
out of reach for least developed countries, the online university or equivalent platform
could become a catalyst for inclusive, equitable and transformative learning.

65. Given the persistent gap in tertiary education across least developed countries,
there is an urgent need to operationalize the proposed online university as a matter of
priority. The initiative would build on existing programmes and transferable best
practices, including those from UNU, that offer valuable insights into delivering
educational programmes and conducting research in science, technology, engineering
and mathematics disciplines. Taking into account that there is no one -size-fits-all
solution for the least developed countries, the unique value of the proposed online
university would lie in its ability to deliver tailored capacity -building approaches to
least developed countries, so they can respond to their national needs for online
science, technology, engineering and mathematics education.

66. The United Nations system is uniquely positioned to lead this effort, leveraging
its convening power to engage a diverse range of stakeholders, including least
developed country Governments, development partners, the private sector, civil
society and academia, in order to advance this initiative for the global common good.
Furthermore, a United Nations-led initiative could provide global visibility, promote
universal access, foster cross-border recognition of credentials and facilitate
educational mobility.

67. The proposed online university or equivalent platform is not envisioned as a
degree-issuing institution. Rather, it will build the capacity of existing higher
education institutions in least developed countries to deliver graduate and
postgraduate science, technology, engineering and mathematics programmes. Its core
objectives would be to facilitate and expand access to high-quality learning
opportunities, in particular for the poorest and most marginalized populations , and
contribute meaningfully to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

68. To address complexities and challenges of quality assurance and accreditation
in least developed countries, the proposed online university would work within the
existing accreditation frameworks and with the quality assurance bodies of those
countries for the immediate recognition of qualifications, while also pursuing regional
and global recognition of qualifications in line with Global Convention on the
Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education.

69. In order for the online university or equivalent platform to operate effectively,
it is essential to ensure solutions for adequate digital infrastructure and Internet
access. In addition, drawing on lessons from the Université numérique Cheikh
Hamidou Kane and other models, it will be important to establish local learning
centres with digital access beyond university campuses, as that would enable students
with no connection to electricity or the Internet to participate in online university
programmes. Additional strategies to improve access and connectivity include
building partnerships with telecommunications companies and other private sector
actors.

70. To achieve meaningful and equitable impact, the proposed online university or
equivalent platform would integrate gender-responsive pedagogical models. It could
establish targeted scholarship programmes and schemes to facilitate participation and
promote academic continuity in remote or under-resourced regions. Furthermore, the
initiative should develop structured pathways for virtual internships, job placement
services and mentorship opportunities. By integrating those components, the
proposed online university would not only broaden access, but also foster
empowerment and the socioeconomic resilience of women, the poorest and
marginalized peoples.

71. Resource mobilization is critical to the success and long-term sustainability of
the proposed online university. To secure necessary funding, the initiative would
pursue innovative partnerships with governments, international organizations, civil
society, academia, think tanks and the private sector. Once fully operational, its
recurrent costs could be supplemented through diversified revenue-generating
streams, including grants, donations and strategic corporate partnerships.

72. Establishing an online university or an equivalent platform dedicated to least
developed countries is not only viable but also urgently needed. Such an initiative
would be a highly effective solution to meeting the growing demand for higher
education in least developed countries. In addition, the initiative would be vital for
building knowledge and taking advantage of the global technological revolution
currently under way, with a view to ensuring that the least developed countries can
benefit from that revolution and are not left behind.

73. Further deliberation is needed to define the precise scope and modalities of the
online university, including its governance structure, partnership frameworks,
funding requirements and sustainability models. A deeper mapping of regional and
country-specific needs through in-country assessments will also be essential. To guide
that process, a dedicated task force should be established to inform the next steps
towards full operationalization of the online university by 2027.
