paragraphs.text: In the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries, which the General Assembly endorsed by its resolution 76/258, Member States committed to undertaking feasibility studies to explore the possibility of establishing an online university or other equivalent platforms to support online graduate and postgraduate university-level science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in least developed countries and recently graduated countries with a view to, inter alia, providing policy support to promote distance education and open learning for graduate and postgraduate studies in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, ensuring a 50/50 gender balance at all levels while guaranteeing special access for the poorest and people in vulnerable situations; creating a virtual network of educational institutions within and beyond least developed countries; assist ing in course design and curriculum development; and leading to scale and sustainability of the education system, taking into account all pre-existing initiatives developed by the relevant partners in a comprehensive manner.

In addition, Member States requested the Secretary-General to submit a report, outlining, inter alia, the mapping of existing initiatives, possible new modalities, resource requirements, accreditation and sustainable funding sources for an online university or other equivalent platforms, to the General Assembly for its consideration.

With a view to fulfilling that mandate, in 2024, the Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States conducted a desk review of the broader higher education landscape. Following the desk review, the Office of the High Representative organized a high-level expert group meeting on the feasibility of establishing an online university for the least developed countries from 3 to 4 June 2025.1 The present report was prepared on the basis of the findings of the desk review, the consultations that the Office held with relevant agencies and entities within the United Nations system and the outcomes of the high-level expert group meeting. In the present report, it is emphasized that establishing an online university for least developed countries is feasible and that such a university is needed in order to enhance access to quality higher education opportunities for the rapidly growing youth populations of such countries.

The proposed online university or equivalent platform is not envisioned as a degree-issuing institution. Instead, its purpose would be to build the capacity of existing institutions in least developed countries to promote graduate and postgraduate science, technology, engineering and mathematics educational initiatives, with an emphasis on expanding access to high -quality learning opportunities for the poorest and marginalized populations, as envisioned in the Doha Programme of Action.

Despite the emergence of numerous initiatives to support online learning in higher education institutions in developing countries, only a few operate at scale or reach women, Indigenous groups, marginalized communities and persons with disabilities. Desk reviews have revealed a glaring gap in online education in least developed countries, with only a handful of institutions offering online science, technology, engineering and mathematics education through digital platforms. In the few cases where institutions offer online programmes, they typically rely on a blended model that incorporates some in-person instruction or requires students to go to community learning centres in order to access to the Internet, technology and faculty. Fully online science, technology, engineering and mathematics education remains virtually non-existent in these countries. These hybrid models reflect ongoing efforts to overcome systemic barriers to access and quality in higher education, but they are isolated examples. Enhanced international cooperation, targeted investment and institutional capacity-building will be essential to advancing inclusive and equitable science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in line with the Doha Programme of Action and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

In view of the persistent and widening gaps in access to higher education in least developed countries, an online university or equivalent platform would offer innovative solutions by deploying cost-effective digital technologies, building strategic partnerships and promoting robust investments to overcome access, geographical and institutional barriers. It would collaborate with existing higher education institutions in least developed countries and foster partnerships with a range of stakeholders to de liver targeted capacity-building, scalable solutions and pathways towards global recognition of science, technology, engineering and mathematics qualifications earned in least developed countries. It holds significant promise as a platform to catalyse efforts aimed at meeting the urgent and growing demand for higher education and unlocking opportunities where they are needed the most.

Relevant United Nations system organizations, in particular, the International Telecommunications Union (ITU), United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), United Nations Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries and United Nations University (UNU), are well placed to provide strategic and technical guidance and support to such an endeavour.

In the present report, the Secretary-General examines the current landscape of science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in least developed countries, highlighting critical gaps in access, quality and delivery. He analyses the underlying challenges and the proposed preliminary solutions aimed at addressing those barriers. In addition, the Secretary-General outlines proposals for advancing the establishment of the proposed online university or equivalent platform and, in that regard, recommends that the Office of the High Representative undertake further consultations in order to define a proposed structure and address governance, resource requirements and other institutional matters.

The least developed countries, which currently number 45, are home to approximately 14 per cent of the global population. In total, 31.4 per cent of the population of the least developed countries live in extreme poverty. Those countries account for only 1.3 per cent of global gross domestic product (GDP), 1.4 per cent of global foreign direct investment and under 1 per cent of global merchandising exports. 2

Under Sustainable Development Goal 4, ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong opportunities for all involves providing education at all levels, from early childhood education to tertiary education, equipping individuals with the skills needed for employment and active participation in society. The working-age (15–64 years) population in least developed countries is expected to double from 610 million in 2020 to 1.2 billion in 2050. This rapid growth makes investing in tertiary education a priority.

The higher education landscape in the least developed countries is evolving and currently undergoing rapid transformation. There is increasing recognition in those countries of the role of higher education in sustainable development. Despite the huge potential and urgency of promoting higher education, least developed countries face major challenges in respect of both increasing access to and improving the quality of higher education. They are in a vicious cycle of low income and low educational opportunities and attainment that results in lack of decent and productive employment. Higher education systems across all least developed countries are characterized by low enrolment rates, limited institutional capacity and significant disparities in access and quality.

Despite notable efforts to make tertiary education more available in least developed countries, the gap in the gross tertiary education enrolment rate between those countries and the rest of the world has continued to grow. The data indicate that, from 2019 to 2023, the gross tertiary education enrolment rate in least developed countries had stagnated at 11.2 per cent, compared with the global average of 43.3 per cent in 2023 (see figure I). Figure I Tertiary education enrolment rate Source: World Bank (2025).

The global higher education gross enrolment ratio masks large disparities between regions of the world. The higher education gross enrolment rat e is highest in Europe and North America, at 75 per cent, and lowest in sub -Saharan Africa, at 8 per cent. 3 There are also wide disparities in enrolment across and within countries, between rural and urban areas and across different segments of the population. For example, in 2023, in sub-Saharan Africa, 78 women were enrolled in higher education for every 100 men, whereas the global ratio was 113 women for every 100 men.4

In the least developed countries, there are approximately 1,530 universities (577 public and 953 private) recognized by the International Association of Universities. That figure accounts for just 7.1 per cent of the 21,580 universities worldwide, highlighting the scarcity of higher education institutions in least developed countries. Moreover, the data reveal a striking disparity in higher education infrastructure between least developed countries and other regions of the world. As at 2025, least developed countries have an average of only 0.61 universities per 100,000 young persons aged 15–29, far below the levels in Europe (4.07), North America (3.20) and Latin America and the Caribbean (2.37) (see figure II). Although certain countries, such as Haiti and Timor-Leste, stand out with relatively better access, the majority, such as Ethiopia (0.18), Bangladesh (0.25) and the United Republic of Tanzania (0.24), are well below the global average. It should be noted that those figures reflect the number of institutions, not their capacity or quality. Figure II Number of universities per 100,000 population aged 15–29 years, 2025 Source: International Association of Universities, World Higher Education Database (2025).

Several interconnected factors, including socioeconomic, structural and cultural challenges, contribute to the low enrolment rate in the least developed countries. In many cases, institutions of higher learning are geographically concentrated in urban centres, limiting the availability of educational services to populations residing in remote and rural areas. This structural imbalance is further compounded by a scarcity of available enrolment spaces, particularly in public universities. Notwithstanding persistent challenges related to financing and infrastructure, public institutions in least developed countries continue to accommodate most tertiary -level students, reflecting their central role in national education systems.

In recent decades, the number of private universities in least developed countries has grown significantly and now exceeds that of public institutions. While private universities play an important role in absorbing demand and alleviating pressure on overstretched public systems, their predominantly tuition-based models often reinforce existing structural inequities in access to higher education. As a result, students from lower-income backgrounds remain disproportionately excluded from opportunities for tertiary education, deepening socioeconomic disparities in least developed countries.

Low educational attainment at the secondary level continues to pose a major impediment to increasing enrolment in tertiary education in least developed countries. This challenge is especially acute among marginalized and displaced groups and lower-income segments of the population, which face compounded barriers to 4.07 3.20 2.37 1.83 3.00 0.61 Europe North America Latin America and the Caribbean Asia and the Pacific Non-least developed countries Least developed countries progression within the education system. As a result, tertiary education enrolment rates in least developed countries continue to lag, constraining the development of a skilled workforce and perpetuating intergenerational cycles of poverty and exclusion.

Owing to the limited number of higher education institutions that are available and accessible, capacity constraints manifest in overcrowded institutions, inadequate infrastructure and a shortage of qualified faculty. These structural limitations not only restrict opportunities for higher education, they also undermine the overall resilience and responsiveness of least developed countries’ higher education systems with regard to meeting the demands of an increasingly dynamic and knowledge -driven global economy.

The capacity challenge extends to the scope of graduate and postgraduate courses available in least developed countries. While enrolment in tertiary education institutions offering science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees has increased, 95.4 per cent of courses in those subjects are being offered in non -least developed countries and only 4.6 per cent in least developed countries, although latter’s share of the global youth population is 18.6 per cent. 5 This disparity (see figure III) highlights the urgent need to expand science, technology, engineering and mathematics education opportunities in least developed countries, in order to support inclusive development and global workforce readiness. Figure III Number of science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees offered by higher education institutions by region, 2025 Source: International Association of Universities, World Higher Education Database (2025).

Higher education, especially in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, is crucial for least developed countries to drive socioeconomic development and achieve parity with more advanced countries. The least developed countries, however, are falling behind in this area. Gender disparities in science, technology, engineering and mathematics are pronounced. Globally, only 35 per cent of graduates in those fields are women because of the barriers posed by overall lower literacy levels among women, societal norms, lack of role models and limited access to technology. Specific data for women in least developed countries are unavailable.

Rapid and often unregulated expansion of higher education institutions has led to overcrowded classrooms, overburdened faculty, declining investment in such critical infrastructure as laboratories and libraries, shrinking academic activities and the deterioration of facilities.6 These conditions have contributed to an erosion in the quality of higher education in many least developed countries.

Both internal and external quality assurance are needed and play an important role in assuring stakeholders that acceptable educational standards are being maintained and enhanced. Despite the launch of several African regional frameworks to promote harmonization of quality assurance and accreditation in higher education, quality assurance in least developed countries remain fragmented owing to a lack of robust national mechanisms, lack of coordination between ministries, universities and regulatory agencies and limited participation in international peer reviews and benchmarking exercises.

According to UNESCO, developed countries have significantly more national quality assurance institutions and national qualification frameworks than most developing countries. Of the approximately 800 higher education quality assurance bodies operating worldwide, only 170 have undergone external evaluation, among which very few are from the least developed countries. 7 Strengthening quality assurance in least developed countries will require capacity-building, strengthening regional collaboration and alignment with global standards, such as those promoted by UNESCO.

The Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education is the first international treaty on the recognition of higher education qualifications. The Convention, which is aimed at streamlining and standardizing the evaluation and acceptance of academic credentials worldwide, could be the impetus needed for countries, including the least developed countries, to embrace a standardized recognition system.

The digital divide is a major structural barrier that further exacerbates the higher education gaps in least developed countries. According to the International Telecommunications Union (ITU), the digital connectivity gap between least developed countries and the rest of the world has widened.8 In 2024, only 35 per cent of people in those countries were online, compared with 68 per cent globally and 93 per cent in high-income countries. Although two thirds of the overall population of the least developed countries is offline, ITU data show, that in 2023, 45 per cent of young persons aged 15–24 in those countries were already online, giving an online learning platform an immediate, sizeable audience while still leaving room for outreach and expansion as connectivity grows. 9 Significant disparities persist between men and women and between rural and urban areas. Only 83 per cent of people in least developed countries are covered by a mobile broadband signal (3G or higher), compared with 95 per cent globally. High Internet costs remain a major barrier, with access in least developed countries costing about four times the global average.10 The lack of access to electricity remains an obstacle in least developed countries attempting to adopt online learning. In 2023, 59 per cent of the population in those countries had access to electricity.11 The challenges relating to the use of online learning in those countries became particularly apparent during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic. Data from World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) studies confirm that learning losses were larger in countries with lower GDP per capita.12,13 While most high-income countries were able to quickly roll out remote teaching and learning, the least developed countries struggled to respond, suspending classes and examinations for an extended period, more than a year in many instances.

While considerable efforts are under way in several least developed countries to bridge the digital divide in higher education, including by strengthening public - private partnerships to invest in the digital infrastructure, such as broadband service and Internet access, bridging the digital divide, in particular in rural areas, where 60 per cent of the least developed country populations live, will require sustained investment and time.14 Given the urgency of ensuring inclusive and equitable access to learning opportunities, interim strategies must be actively pursued, including the deployment of offline learning tools, the adaptation of digital platforms for low - bandwidth environments and the creation of public access hubs to support community-based learning, with a view to providing crucial tools to ensure progress in education inclusion.

The low level of investment in higher education in least developed countries is a key factor contributing to both the limited availability and the broader quality challenges of tertiary education. In total, least developed countries spen t approximately $51 billion on education in 2024, representing 3.2 per cent of their GDP, compared with $4.2 trillion globally, which accounts for 3.8 per cent of global GDP. Specifically, for tertiary education, least developed countries allocate d 20.3 per cent of their government education expenditure, amounting to just $10.4 billion, while global spending on tertiary education is estimated at $908.4 billion. 15 Globally, spending on tertiary education amounts to 1.1 per cent of government expenditure in the least developed countries, although those countries account for 14 per cent of the global population and 18.8 per cent of the global youth population. Those figures underscore the limited financial resources available for education in least developed countries, in particular for higher education, which affects the quality, accessibility and capacity of the education systems in those countries.

Total education aid at the global level reached a record high of $16.6 billion in 2022. The proportion of official development assistance (ODA) directed towards education, however, declined from 9.3 per cent in 2019 to 7.6 per cent in 2022. 16 Of the total ODA received, the largest portion was directed towards basic education (46 per cent), followed by post-secondary education (28 per cent) and secondary education (26 per cent). In 2023, total ODA allocated to scholarships costs reached $4.6 billion, marking a 31 per cent increase since 2015.17 Of that sum, $385.3 million was directed to least developed countries and, notably, students pursuing science, technology, engineering and mathematics education accounted for almost 30 per cent of global scholarship recipients.18

Only 30 per cent of education aid provided by the 10 largest donors to sub-Saharan Africa was disbursed directly to recipient countries. The remaining 70 per cent was channelled through donor aid agencies, international and domestic non-governmental organizations and multilateral organizations.19 This indirect allocation often results in fragmentation and lack of government leadership, underscoring the need for adequate, efficient and equitable investment in education, especially in countries with great gaps. In addition, students from least developed countries are almost twice as likely t o pursue tertiary education abroad compared with their peers from other countries. Consequently, they are more likely to take skilled jobs overseas, increasing the risk of brain drain .

Public spending on education is highly unequal within countries globally, with the top income quintiles capturing a disproportionate share of available resources. In a 2024 report, the World Bank and UNESCO noted that inequalities tend to be highest in poorer countries, such as the least developed countries, where differences in enrolment patterns by income quintile is most unequal for tertiary education, as those with access to this level of education mainly come from wealthier households. As a result, wealthier households receive a much higher share of public expenditure for higher education compared with poorer households. The World Bank and UNESCO also found that funding for secondary and tertiary education becomes more equitable as enrolment increases at the primary and secondary levels among the poor.20

While the terms open university and online university are often used interchangeably, they denote distinct models within the higher education landscape. Open universities are primarily defined by their commitment to open access and characterized by minimal entry requirements, lack of age restrictions and inclusive policies aimed at democratizing education for non-traditional learners, including working adults, individuals in remote or rural areas and marginalized populations. A principal point of differentiation lies in their respective modes of delivery. Online universities focus predominantly on digital platforms, offering education primarily through virtual means with structured online curricula. By contrast, open universities frequently employ a broader range of instructional modalities, including printed materials, radio and television broadcasts and localized learning support centres, enabling flexible and multichannel access to education.

Open and distance learning has become a central global strategy to broaden access to education, in particular in developing countries. In recent years, the increasing demand for higher education coupled with greater access to the Internet has led to the introduction of distance blended and online learning as new ways of teaching and learning, providing more flexibility for learners.

A key component of this changing educational landscape is the development of open educational resources, which may include digital resources, such as e-textbooks, and videos and virtual labs that are licenced for free educational use and easily accessible online. Open educational resources are digital public goods available on an open copyright licence that respects the intellectual property rights of the copyright owner and allow users to re-use, repurpose, adapt and redistribute such resources. Open solutions that use open educational resources are crucial to supporting the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

Massive online open courses are another recent development in education. Between 2011 and 2021, the number of learners reached by such courses increased from 300,000 to 220 million around the world, excluding China. 21 In 2021, a total of 40 million new learners signed up for at least one massive online open course. No prior qualifications are required to enrol in massive online open courses. Such course s, however, are not necessarily open educational resources. While some of the world’s leading universities, such as MIT and Harvard, offer massive online open courses, the fees for the certification track can be a significant access barrier for learners fro m low- income backgrounds in developing countries. Many of the most popular massive online open courses cannot be reused without permission from the original provider. Massive online open courses mainly benefit learners from richer countries owing to divides in digital skills, Internet access, language and course design. A study of higher educa tion repositories with open educational resource collections found that nearly 90 per cent were created in Europe or North America and that 92 per cent of the material in the OER Commons global library is in English, which affects who can use such content. 22

Developing countries and least developed countries, in particular, face a unique set of challenges in broadening access to massive online open courses and open educational resources. A systematic review of the research into the use of open online learning technologies in developing countries context reveals five interrelated barriers or challenges: (a) access to the Internet; (b) digital literacy; (c) online pedagogies; (d) the context of content; and (e) flow of knowledge between North and South. 23

Offering science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees fully online at the undergraduate or graduate level remains a challenge owing to the need for laboratory work; there are no official data available for courses in those fields. Some open universities have addressed that challenge by using television or video to demonstrate lab work. Blended models of science, technology, engineering and mathematics courses are more common, whereby students attend their laboratory classes in person at designated facilities. More recently, digital simulations have been developed to demonstrate scientific processes that are difficult to replicate in a traditional laboratory, while virtual labs enable students to remotely control laboratory equipment. The Remote Access to Laboratory Equipment initiative of UNESCO is helping to bridge that gap by enabling scientists and students in under - resourced regions, in particular in Africa, to gain access to and operate advanced scientific instruments remotely, often for the first time. This initiative not only facilitates remote experimentation but also provides structured training and technical support, thereby building sustainable local capacity and empowering researchers to conduct high-quality science from their home institutions. While digital simulations and virtual labs are usually expensive to develop, once created, they are sometimes offered as open educational resources.

In recent years, there have been major developments in the use of artificial intelligence in education. While artificial intelligence systems are evolving rapidly, often outpacing regulation and sometimes without adequate safeguards or quality assurance, their educational application could offer substantial benefits. Artificial intelligence-driven solutions have demonstrated substantial benefits, in particular in the following areas: (a) Accelerated development of undergraduate curricula, in particular in science, technology, engineering and mathematics education, through data -informed instructional design; (b) Adaptive learning platforms that deliver personalized educational content based on individual learning styles and progress; (c) Real-time feedback and continuous academic support tailored to meet the unique needs of individual learners; (d) Streamlined and automated student assessments, enhancing efficiency and consistency in evaluation; (e) Personalized career guidance, helping students make informed decisions based on their strengths, interests and employment trends.

The appropriate use of artificial intelligence in online education offers significant potential for cost savings in course design and delivery, while also enhancing the learning experience. The quality of online learning can vary widely, however, as in th e case of traditional classroom teaching. More than 30 years of experience in online education has led to the emergence of a set of best practices emphasizing the importance of clear course structure, defined weekly learning objectives, manageable study workloads, active engagement, assignment deadlines and regular feedback. Collaborative learning among students has also been shown to improve outcomes.

Integrating artificial intelligence into teaching and learning will make it possible not only to leverage artificial intelligence to improve the design and delivery of online courses, but also to develop explicit instructions on the responsible and effecti ve use of artificial intelligence tools, thereby reducing the cost of design and delivery of online courses as well. Training educators to effectively use artificial intelligence tools can enhance instructional design, automate assessments and deliver personalized feedback. At the same time, equipping students with digital literacy skills prepares them to engage with artificial intelligence-powered tools and intelligent tutoring systems using real-time application of artificial intelligence to support the delivery of individualized learning pathways, thereby enabling both educators and learners to become not only beneficiaries of education that is enhanced by the use of artificial intelligence, but also informed participants in shaping its future.

In addition to conducting a desk review of online education and holding bilateral consultations, the Office of the High Representative organized a high-level expert group meeting at United Nations Headquarters in New York on 3 and 4 June 2025. The meeting brought together 24 distinguished global experts, including several from least developed countries, with expertise in online and higher education, artificial intelligence, digital transformation, policy and science, technology, engineering and mathematics curriculum development. Participants represented the United Nations system, least developed country Governments, academia, philanthropic foundations and the private sector. The meeting, which was organized in close collaboration with UNESCO and UNU, benefited from the active participation and strong support of Member States, including the Permanent Representatives of Bangladesh, the Gambia, Malawi, Nepal, Timor-Leste, Türkiye and Tuvalu, as well as a representative of Qatar.24 The closing session was open to all Member States and drew significant attention and engagement.

Pursuant to the mandate set out in the Doha Programme of Action, the meeting was held in order to guide the development of feasibility studies for the establishment of an online university or equivalent platform. The programme of the meeting was structured around five core thematic areas identified as essential to the effective conceptualization of the proposed initiative: (a) mapping of existing initiatives; (b) possible new modalities; (c) resource requirements; (d) quality assurance and accreditation; and (e) sustainable funding sources. One of the cross-cutting themes of the meeting was ensuring gender balance at all levels while guaranteeing access for the poorest and people in vulnerable situations and avoiding duplication of efforts.

In recent years, a growing number of initiatives have emerged to support the advancement of distance and online learning in higher education institutions in developing countries. More than 20 relevant initiatives were identified during the preparation of the present report, reflecting an expanding landscape of innovation that is aimed at improving access to tertiary education. Mapping efforts reveal a modest but growing number of open and online universities operating in least developed countries. Many of those institutions have adopted blended learning models, combining elements of both open and online universities. They are pioneering new approaches to distance education across a range of disciplines, in particular in teacher training, public policy and information technology. Only a limited number of those institutions, however, currently offer fully accredited online science, technology, engineering and mathematics degree programmes. Those that do often rely on a mix of instructional methods, rather than using virtual platforms specifically built to deliver the entire course structure online, thus highlighting a persistent gap in the provision of science, technology, engineering and mathematics education at scale in least developed countries.

The two largest initiatives reviewed in terms of number of students were the Bangladesh Open University, with has more than 1 million students, including some outside the country, and the University of the People, which is based in the United States of America. The latter is a fully online university with 153,000 students from 209 countries, including 35,000 students in the least developed countries. Both institutions emphasize flexibility, affordability and accessibility, in particular for underserved populations.

The African Virtual University, a pan-African intergovernmental institution, is helping African countries to implement online learning. The African Virtual University was established by African Governments with a mandate to significantly increase access to quality higher education and training through the innovative use of information and communications technology (ICT). Other areas in which the University has been involved include designing and implementing e -learning projects, training instructors for e-learning platforms and providing resources for managing a digital library. It has trained 43,000 graduates and has 31 learning centres in 17 countries, of which 14 are in least developed countries.

The Université numérique Cheikh Hamidou Kane, based in Senegal, offers public online university degree courses accredited at the national and African levels in science, technology, engineering and mathematics using an innovative model. Accredited by the national quality assurance authority for higher education of Senegal and recognized at the regional level by the African and Malagasy Council for Higher Education, the Université numérique Cheikh Hamidou Kane offers a strategic model for scalable digital higher education that can be replicated in the resource-constrained contexts of least developed countries. In 2025, the university had an enrolment exceeding 74,000 students, with approximately 44 per cent of its academic offerings concentrated in science, technology, engineering and digital innovation. The university’s master’s degree programmes include such specialized fields as big data analysis, ICT security, artificial intelligence, robotics and advanced mathematics, demonstrating a commitment to developing students with future-ready skills and contributing to national and regional knowledge economies. 25

A few least developed countries have open universities, such as the Open University of Liberia and the Open University of the Sudan. Both use a blended model to deliver academic programmes in which students access digital materials, use print materials and take part in face-to-face sessions. The reach and impact of online tertiary education in least developed countries remain difficult to quantify owing to limited data. Moreover, standardized indicators for online education, such as enrolment, outcomes and completion rates, are largely unavailable for least developed countries, hindering global comparisons and making benchmarking difficult.

The United Nations has a number of relevant initiatives. UNU, while primarily mandated to promote research, offers master’s and doctoral programmes directed at the nationals of developing countries, including least developed countries. In 2024, UNU had 321 postgraduate students enrolled across its 13 institutes in 12 countries. Of that number, 54 per cent from developing countries and 64 per cent were women. 26 UNU also provides online and blended courses that have the potential to reach remote learners. Its academic focus spans biotechnology, environment, frontier technologies, sustainability, global health and natural resource management in Africa, among other fields. While UNU grants postgraduate degrees in the public policy domains, none of its partner institutions are from the least developed countries. In addition, the UNESCO Institute for Information Technologies in Education promotes the innovative use of ICT and serves as a facilitator and enabler for achieving Sustainable Development Goal 4 (quality education) through ICT-enabled solutions and best practices. UNESCO also promotes the Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education to help countries develop their own quality assurance agencies.

The Commonwealth of Learning is helping its constituent States, including 14 least developed countries, and institutions to use distance learning and technologies for expanding access to education and training. It works with ministries and higher education institutions to increase equitable access to quality tertiary education, promotes the rapid design, development and delivery of quality gender-responsive open educational resources and assists in the development and implementation of employability frameworks.

Several international higher education networks, such as the Pan African University, the International Network of Higher Education in Africa, the Asian Association of Open Universities and the International Association of Universities, among others, support distance and online learning and promote collaboration to enhance the quality of distance learning, including by occasionally sharing open educational resources. None of these entities, however, provide degrees in science, technology, engineering and mathematics. There are also a number of civil society organizations and education entrepreneurs that could provide valuable support, such as Maktab93, a free online school for Afghan students, especially girls who have been deprived of formal education, and BAG Innovation, a for-profit organization that has developed, in collaboration with universities and employers in East Africa, an online system to complement theoretical learning with practical experience before students graduate.

Those initiatives help to expand online education in developing countries, in particular in Africa and the least developed countries, and offer valuable experience and expertise. Partnering with them would help facilitate the delivery of online science, technology, engineering and mathematics degrees and courses in least developed countries.

In examining modalities for the establishment of an online university or equivalent platform to bridge the higher education gap in least developed countries, four strategic models were considered. There are distinct advantages and operational considerations associated with each model (see table).

Each option involves trade-offs related to scalability, contextual relevance and institutional capacity-building in the least developed countries. Among the options considered, a hybrid model combining options B and C emerged as the most balanced and cost-effective pathway for the proposed online university or equivalent platform to deliver online science, technology, engineering and mathematics education. Under this model, local universities in least developed countries would form an interconnected network supported by the United Nations and strengthened by partnerships with existing regional and global networks and global academic institutions. By anchoring delivery in the local context, this approach promotes both relevance and resilience. It would also help foster regional cooperation and capacity- building by offering a scalable and sustainable solution to meet the growing demand for science, technology, engineering and mathematics education across least developed countries.

Establishing a United Nations online university or equivalent platform will require the deployment of financial and technical resources in order to find solutions for existing gaps in digital infrastructure and address access barriers faced by least developed countries. The entity would need funding not only to cover its administrative costs, but also to facilitate and support the development of digital platforms, instructional design, virtual laboratories and offline -compatible systems; partner with global academic experts to facilitate capacity-building of faculty in least developed countries, blended preparatory programmes for digital literacy and study skills; and develop multilingual course materials that are contextually relevant and responsive to local labour markets. Artificial intelligence-powered platforms have significant potential to deliver high-quality science, technology, engineering and mathematics content to remote areas, bypassing infrastructure limitations. Artificial intelligence tools can also generate major cost-savings in content adaptation, customize learning materials and automate updates, making content accessible to a wide range of end users. A strong focus on developing and expanding digital literacy, especially among women, marginalized groups, instructors and policymakers, will be essential to ensure inclusion and long-term impact in relation to science, technology, engineering and mathematics education.

Lack of digital connectivity is a fundamental challenge to any online learning initiative for least developed countries. Internet access is essential not only for educational purposes but also for economic development. This barrier can only be removed through coordinated action by least developed country Governments, international agencies and telecommunications companies. Reliable and seamless access to the Internet is a necessary prerequisite for the execution of online learning.

Currently, there is a significant variation in qualifications and accreditation mechanisms across least developed countries. As a result, it is difficult to have academic credentials transferred to and recognized in other countries. Online degrees, in particular those offered across borders, are often met with considerable scepticism by employers and local academic institutions and are not recognized at all, in many cases. This is largely because there are no national policy frameworks in place that make it possible to formally recognize or accredit foreign or online qualifications. In addition, many universities in least developed countries lack the administrative and pedagogical infrastructure necessary to support blended or online partnerships with international education providers.

Moreover, the recognition of online degrees in certain science, technology, engineering and mathematics disciplines by regulatory authorities remains a significant challenge. Even when students complete online programmes, their credentials are often not widely accepted by employers or government bodies. Without formal recognition from national accreditation bodies, these qualifications often carry limited value in local job markets. Accreditation should be viewed as a continuum, rather than a binary process, with microcredentials serving as building blocks leading to formal recognition.

To address those challenges, strategies must be developed to navigate multi-country accreditation processes, including the adoption of global, regional and national accreditation frameworks. An online university or equivalent platform can play a key role in supporting efforts towards building capacity to harmonize quality assurance checks, adhering to international standards and advancing the ratification of Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education. In collaboration with UNESCO, the online university or equivalent platform should adopt and implement a rigorous quality assessment for all least developed country science, technology, engineering and mathematics programmes that receive funding or support through an online university or equivalent platform.

To ensure financial resilience and sustainability, the online university or equivalent platform should seek to diversify its funding sources to include grants and donations. It should establish knowledge partnerships with academic institutions for pedagogical innovation, curriculum development and quality assurance, public - private partnerships for infrastructure, connectivity and technology solutions. Strengthening government engagement will be critical, as national authorities must play a central role in supporting and scaling such initiatives. To ensure equitable access, especially for those left furthest behind, scholarship schemes and targeted financial support should also be considered.

A deeper review of successful models, such as the Université numérique Cheikh Hamidou Kane, the University of the People and Smart Education Platform of China, reveals that they offer practical lessons in scaling access, leveraging blended delivery and ensuring employability. Education Above All offers a comprehensive package of support, including free access to education, digital tools, financial assistance and tailored programmes through innovative partnerships and funding models. Those approaches should be further explored to inform the design of online university or equivalent platform.

Broad-based collaboration with United Nations entities will also be required to leverage and build on existing capacities. Key entities, including ITU, UNESCO, the United Nations Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries and UNU, are well positioned to contribute to science, technology, engineering and mathematics advancement in least developed countries and support the online university or equivalent platform.

The working-age population (15–64 years) in least developed countries is projected to double from 610 million in 2020 to 1.2 billion in 2050. This demographic shift presents a potential opportunity to realize large, sustained demographic dividends driven by declining dependency ratios and expanding labour forces. It is not a certainty, however, that it will be possible to take advantage of this opportunity. Without access to quality education and decent employment, the potential dividend could be lost, leading to increased inequality and social instability, instead.

Least developed countries possess abundant renewable energy and human potential, but they lack the capacity to fully harness them for development. Investment in science, technology, engineering and mathematics education is therefore essential not only to building the foundations of a knowledge-based economy, but also to preparing for the transformative impact of such emerging technologies as generative artificial intelligence and big data. Higher education in science, technology, engineering and mathematics offers the least developed countries a unique opportunity to leapfrog traditional development models and shift directly to service-based economies.

Existing online degree platforms largely fail to meet the needs of the populations in least developed countries owing to systemic and multifaceted barriers that make quality science, technology, engineering and mathematics education inaccessible. Infrastructure deficits, limited institutional capacity and high costs associated with traditional models compound the challenge. Cultural and linguistic barriers further exclude potential learners, while gender disparities intensify exclusion, as evidenced by the fact that only 19 per cent of women in least developed countries use the Internet.

The proposed online university or equivalent platform could play a pivotal role in bridging the digital and educational divide, in particular in science, technology, engineering and mathematics fields. It could help strengthen digital infrastructure development, human capital formation and quality assurance systems through international cooperation, thereby narrowing the higher education enrolment gaps in least developed countries. By brokering strategic partnerships that may otherwise be out of reach for least developed countries, the online university or equivalent platform could become a catalyst for inclusive, equitable and transformative learning.

Given the persistent gap in tertiary education across least developed countries, there is an urgent need to operationalize the proposed online university as a matter of priority. The initiative would build on existing programmes and transferable best practices, including those from UNU, that offer valuable insights into delivering educational programmes and conducting research in science, technology, engineering and mathematics disciplines. Taking into account that there is no one -size-fits-all solution for the least developed countries, the unique value of the proposed online university would lie in its ability to deliver tailored capacity -building approaches to least developed countries, so they can respond to their national needs for online science, technology, engineering and mathematics education.

The United Nations system is uniquely positioned to lead this effort, leveraging its convening power to engage a diverse range of stakeholders, including least developed country Governments, development partners, the private sector, civil society and academia, in order to advance this initiative for the global common good. Furthermore, a United Nations-led initiative could provide global visibility, promote universal access, foster cross-border recognition of credentials and facilitate educational mobility.

The proposed online university or equivalent platform is not envisioned as a degree-issuing institution. Rather, it will build the capacity of existing higher education institutions in least developed countries to deliver graduate and postgraduate science, technology, engineering and mathematics programmes. Its core objectives would be to facilitate and expand access to high-quality learning opportunities, in particular for the poorest and most marginalized populations , and contribute meaningfully to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

To address complexities and challenges of quality assurance and accreditation in least developed countries, the proposed online university would work within the existing accreditation frameworks and with the quality assurance bodies of those countries for the immediate recognition of qualifications, while also pursuing regional and global recognition of qualifications in line with Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education.

In order for the online university or equivalent platform to operate effectively, it is essential to ensure solutions for adequate digital infrastructure and Internet access. In addition, drawing on lessons from the Université numérique Cheikh Hamidou Kane and other models, it will be important to establish local learning centres with digital access beyond university campuses, as that would enable students with no connection to electricity or the Internet to participate in online university programmes. Additional strategies to improve access and connectivity include building partnerships with telecommunications companies and other private sector actors.

To achieve meaningful and equitable impact, the proposed online university or equivalent platform would integrate gender-responsive pedagogical models. It could establish targeted scholarship programmes and schemes to facilitate participation and promote academic continuity in remote or under-resourced regions. Furthermore, the initiative should develop structured pathways for virtual internships, job placement services and mentorship opportunities. By integrating those components, the proposed online university would not only broaden access, but also foster empowerment and the socioeconomic resilience of women, the poorest and marginalized peoples.

Resource mobilization is critical to the success and long-term sustainability of the proposed online university. To secure necessary funding, the initiative would pursue innovative partnerships with governments, international organizations, civil society, academia, think tanks and the private sector. Once fully operational, its recurrent costs could be supplemented through diversified revenue-generating streams, including grants, donations and strategic corporate partnerships.

Establishing an online university or an equivalent platform dedicated to least developed countries is not only viable but also urgently needed. Such an initiative would be a highly effective solution to meeting the growing demand for higher education in least developed countries. In addition, the initiative would be vital for building knowledge and taking advantage of the global technological revolution currently under way, with a view to ensuring that the least developed countries can benefit from that revolution and are not left behind.

Further deliberation is needed to define the precise scope and modalities of the online university, including its governance structure, partnership frameworks, funding requirements and sustainability models. A deeper mapping of regional and country-specific needs through in-country assessments will also be essential. To guide that process, a dedicated task force should be established to inform the next steps towards full operationalization of the online university by 2027.

The General Assembly, taking into account the findings and conclusions set out in the present report, may wish to consider the following recommendations: (a) Support efforts to further elaborate the structure and governance mechanisms of and address other institutional matters related to the online university and conduct a sample mapping of in-country assessments in collaboration with relevant United Nations entities, including UNESCO, the United Nations Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries and UNU, in order to evaluate national readiness for implementing or expanding online and blended education. These assessments should focus on such key areas as digital infrastructure, curriculum development and accreditation, digital literacy among faculty and students and availability of online laboratory facilities. The goal is to identify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and challenges within each country’s education and digital ecosystem. Furthermore, the mapping should evaluate instructional design requirements, including offline access and multilingual content delivery, integration of open education resources and artificial intelligence-enabled solutions, in order to uphold the principle of universality and rapidly scale up the delivery of inclusive and quality science, technology, engineering and mathematics education in least developed countries; (b) Establish a task force, to be supported by the Office of the High Representative, that would provide strategic direction leading towards full operationalization of the online university. The membership of the task force should include relevant representatives from the United Nations system, government representatives and experts. Representatives of other relevant stakeholders and organizations may be invited to participate in the work of the task force, in order to promote an exchange of views and enable them to provide inputs, as required; (c) Commit to advancing the modalities of the proposed online university by strategically leveraging existing facilities and resources in the United Nations system, including the academic and research infrastructure provided by such entities as ITU, UNESCO, the United Nations Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries and UNU, as well as other relevant institutions, and also through external partnerships; (d) Endorse the above steps towards the establishment of an online university or equivalent platform for least developed countries in accordance with the Doha Programme of Action, with a view to formally launching the online university at the mid-term review of the Programme of Action in 2027.

Summary
The present report was prepared in response to General Assembly resolution
80/129 entitled “Follow-up to and implementation of the outcomes of the
International Conferences on Financing for Development”. The report presents
progress and challenges in the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment across the
action areas of the Financing for Development outcomes and in the context of growing

I. Introduction

1. In its resolution 80/129, the General Assembly requested the Secretary-General
to submit a report to the Assembly at its eighty-first session on the follow-up to and
the implementation of the Financing for Development outcomes and the Sevilla
Commitment, including on progress made and continuing challenges faced.

2. In the context of growing volatility, more frequent and extreme shocks and
geoeconomic fragmentation, the present report presents progress and challenges in
the implementation of the Financing for Development outcomes, with particular
emphasis on the effects of crises on the financing agenda and on possible financing
policy responses, at both the national and international levels.

II. Financing for development in a more crisis-prone world

3. The Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development took place
in a challenging context, characterized by rising trade and geopolitical tensions, more
frequent and intense climate shocks and a difficult macroeconomic environment.
Developing countries, particularly the poorest and most vulnerable, are facing a
financing squeeze; in a period of tepid global growth, progress on mobilizing
additional domestic resources has been limited, with convergence between
developing and developed countries stalling after the coronavirus disease
(COVID-19) pandemic; foreign direct investment showed resilience in 2025, but
increased by only 2 per cent in developing countries, after falls in earlier years; a
sharp drop in official development assistance (ODA), trade turbulence, high costs of
capital and historically high debt service burdens further add to financing challenges. 1

4. These challenges have been exacerbated by a series of shocks in recent years.
These shocks have had significant macroeconomic and financing repercussions, often
affecting countries in a highly uneven manner. The conflict in the Middle East and
the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is only the latest such example, with impacts
determined by countries’ exposure to its core transmission channels (energy markets,
fertilizers and other supply chains and financial flows) and their capacity to respond.
Many energy-importing developing economies face new growth headwinds,
inflationary pressures and balance-of-payments strains. While countries in Asia are
most exposed to the energy shock, countries in Africa and least developed countries
are highly vulnerable to rising food prices and also have the least capacity to
implement macroeconomic responses, in view of limited fiscal space or external
buffers. Depending on the length of the conflict, its spillovers could become much
more damaging, testing the institutions providing the global financial safety net.2

5. The Sevilla Commitment renewed the global framework for financing for
development and updated the agenda to make it fit for purpose for a more crisis-prone
world. It contains commitments to address the financing squeeze and debt
sustainability pressures, increase financial flows and investment in sustainable
development and the Sustainable Development Goals, strengthen countries’ resilience
and make the international financial architecture better equipped to support countries
in addressing current challenges and absorbing future shocks. This includes stepping
up investment in crisis prevention and resilience, scaling up pre -arranged financing
and instruments that provide automatic breathing space during shocks and
strengthening the global financial safety net, among other actions.

6. The financing for development agenda is holistic, with policies across all action
areas required to sustainably and significantly increase financing and investment. It
also balances actions at the domestic and international levels: country leadership is a
key cross-cutting principle, while the international community is responsible for
creating an enabling international economic environment. The Sevilla Commitment
includes a strong package of actions on reform of the international financial, debt and
development cooperation architectures, but also includes steps to strengthen national
leadership in implementation, for example, by placing integrated national financing
frameworks at the centre of efforts and by encouraging countries to appoint national
focal points for financing for development.

7. The implementation of the Sevilla Commitment is taken forward by a wide
range of actors. Some actions require global action and multilateral agreement or are
taken forward within the United Nations, while others can be taken forward by
coalitions of stakeholders. The Sevilla Platform for Action hosts 130 such coalitions,
which have been directly supporting the implementation of 170 actions.

8. The Sevilla Commitment also strengthened the financing for development
follow-up process; this report supports this follow-up by providing an assessment of
progress made and challenges in its implementation, in each of the action areas. It
puts emphasis on how external shocks and the existing gaps in the international
financial architecture have impacted this implementation and makes
recommendations on how the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment can help
address these.

III. Implementation of the Sevilla Commitment in a challenging
global context

A. Domestic public resources

9. In the Sevilla Commitment it is recognized that mobilizing and effectively using
domestic resources is a cornerstone of national ownership, long -term resilience and
funding of public goods. An integrated reform agenda is set out in order to enhance
fiscal systems, improve international tax cooperation, combat illicit financial flows
and strengthen the role of national development banks.

10. The conflict in the Middle East, however, has compounded existing pressures
on domestic public resources, particularly in non-oil-producing countries. Declining
growth rates and disrupted trade flows are eroding tax bases. Many Governments have
cut fuel taxes and introduced or expanded subsidies to protect households from rising
inflationary pressures. According to an International Energy Agency policy response
tracker, as at early June 2026, 54 countries had lowered energy taxes while 31
countries had increased fuel subsidies.3 For the most vulnerable countries, including
least developed countries, constrained fiscal space risks limiting their capacity to
finance the Sustainable Development Goals precisely when needs are most acute. On
the other hand, some net exporting countries may also experience temporary gains
from higher oil, natural gas or fertilizer prices. In such cases, the resulting windfall
revenues should be managed prudently. Oil companies are expected to reap windfall
profits, which can be taxed. Experience from 2022 shows that such windfall taxes can
generate revenues without raising consumer prices, thus supporting the rebuilding of
fiscal buffers, strengthening macroeconomic stability and mobilizing resources.

11. Structural tax capacity challenges long predate the current conflict. Although
tax revenues have increased over time in both developed and developing countries,
large gaps persist: by 2024, the median tax-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio in
developed countries stood approximately 10 percentage points above that of
developing countries. Some narrowing occurred between 2017 and 2020, but
convergence stalled after the COVID-19 pandemic through uneven recovery paths.
Today, 76 countries collect tax revenues below the 15 per cent of GDP threshold set
in the Sevilla Commitment as a minimum floor.4

12. Advancing domestic public resources mobilization will require sustained
domestic efforts alongside scaled-up international support, through demand-driven
capacity-building, technical assistance and effective cooperation to counter tax
avoidance and illicit flows. Prior to the most recent cuts in ODA, support for domestic
revenue mobilization had grown but remained modest at $1.12 billion in 2024. 5 In the
Sevilla Commitment, development partners were called upon to double their support
in this area by 2030. While data to assess the implementation of this commitment is
not yet available, scaled-up capacity support is the focus of 33 voluntary initiatives
in this action area under the Sevilla Platform for Action.

13. There has been some concrete progress in the areas of international tax
cooperation and combating of illicit financial flows. Member States have engaged
constructively in negotiations on the United Nations framework convention on
international tax cooperation, working on zero drafts ahead of the fifth session in
August 2026. The Economic and Social Council convened its first -ever special
meeting on financial integrity at United Nations Headquarters in New York on
4 February 2026, with a focus on two linked themes: (i) strengthening global
coordination on policy and norm-setting for exchange of information and data; and
(ii) enhancing enforcement capacities and innovation on the use of information and
data. The meeting fostered dialogue among Member States and a broad range of
intergovernmental bodies and stakeholders working across tax cooperation,
anti-money-laundering and anti-corruption frameworks. Participants called for
addressing structural asymmetries in access to information, prioritizing enhancing
interoperability of data systems, promoting whole-of-government approaches at the
national level and supporting integrated capacity development.

14. In the Sevilla Commitment a strong emphasis was placed on the role of public
development banks, as a key lever to mobilize affordable long-term financing. In this
context, it commits to several actions to realize the full potential of national public
development banks. Such public development banks are widespread, but their footprint
varies greatly. While present in a majority of countries, vulnerable countries, such as
the least developed countries and small island developing States have lowest coverage,
with only around two thirds of them having a national public development bank .

B. Domestic and international private business and finance

15. Private business activity, investment and innovation are important drivers of
sustainable development. Nonetheless, global investment growth remains uneven and
concentrated in a small number of countries and sectors, particularly in key
technology sectors, such as artificial intelligence. Despite increased attention to
innovative finance instruments, such as blended finance and some growing adoption
of sustainable business and finance legislation, investment in sustainable
development has fallen short of expectations.

16. Increased geopolitical uncertainty has affected private sector activity and
affected the outlook for foreign direct investment, as some companies have postponed
or cancelled specific projects. Micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises are
particularly vulnerable to related price shocks as they are less able to absorb rising
operational costs due to smaller margins and lower reserves. Countries with large
migrant workforce present in countries affected by conflict have also witnessed
falling inflows in remittances due to a downturn in labour markets in the workers’
host countries.

17. In this challenging context, the Sevilla Commitment includes commitments to
address key barriers to greater private investment in the Sustainable Development
Goals. First, underdeveloped financial and capital markets in many developing
countries which contribute to insufficient access to finance, particularly for women,
marginalized groups and micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises; and second, the
continued misalignment between short-term financial incentives and long-term
sustainable development impact, as well as the high cost of foreign exchange hedging,
which call for a new approach to private capital mobilization.

18. Domestic efforts to implement the Sevilla Commitment are advancing against
the backdrop of rising uncertainties in the global economy. Domestic financial
markets in many developing countries face heightened risks related to rising debt
sustainability challenges, increased market volatility and currency and capital outflow
pressures. To tackle these vulnerabilities, countries should intensify efforts to build
robust domestic financial markets, prioritizing the building of a strong domestic
savings base and domestic and local banking sectors, before introducing more
complex financial markets and instruments that risk being illiquid, underutilized and
more prone to external shocks. Efforts should focus on strengthening the micro -,
small and medium-sized enterprises ecosystem, particularly local, savings and
cooperative banks, as well as national development banks, which play a critical role
in unlocking lending for micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises in local
currency. Complementary actions to facilitate lending in local currencies, including
efforts by multilateral development banks and other public development banks to
build a shared pool of local currencies that reduces the cost of hedging, can support
such efforts. The reversal in remittance flows due to the conflict in the Middle East
has also put a renewed spotlight on efforts to reduce the cost of remittances.

19. Regarding private capital mobilization, blended finance continues to grow in
importance but remains below expectations and concentrated in specific countries and
sectors, largely bypassing countries most in need. Over the period from 2015 to 2024,
private finance mobilized through blended finance grew from $32 billion to
$75 billion.6 Volumes mobilized were four times higher in middle-income countries
than in the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small
island developing States combined.7 Several initiatives under the Sevilla Platform for
Action have begun to tackle these issues. They are showing early results in capital
mobilization through tailored solutions, including foreign exchange hedging,
insurance, grants and technical assistance. An increased focus on alignment with
country priorities, more effective design and use of instruments, increased
collaboration across the blended finance ecosystem and improved data can lead to
scaled-up private capital mobilization and greater impact.

20. Sustainable finance continues to mature as a field, gaining grounds in some
major developing markets – especially across the Asia-Pacific region – even as it
faces backlash in others. Yet, gaps remain that require both innovative mechanisms
to realign private incentives with sustainable development – such as blended finance

C. International development cooperation and
development effectiveness

21. The Sevilla Commitment recognizes the significant contribution of international
development cooperation to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while
acknowledging that it has not kept pace with rising and evolving needs of developing
countries. Amid mutually reinforcing global challenges and increasingly frequent
shocks, demands on international development cooperation are rising, while available
resources, including ODA, are declining, with fewer resources reaching developing
countries. In 2025, ODA provided by member and associates of the Organisation for
Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Development Assistance
Committee fell by 23.1 per cent in real terms compared with 2024, to $174.3 billion,
representing the largest annual drop in the history of ODA. These cuts occurred after
a 7.1 per cent fall in 2024 and are projected to be followed by a further decline in
ODA of 6 per cent in 2026, despite growing needs. 8 This historic fall in ODA is
disproportionately affecting the poorest countries, where ODA remains macrocritical.
In least developed countries, where bilateral ODA represents on average 15 per cent
of Government revenues, ODA fell by 25.8 per cent in 2025, with direct impacts on
their ability to finance their sustainable development.

22. The Sevilla Commitment includes a series of actions to help to bridge the gap
between falling supply and rising demand for international development cooperation:
emphasizing the importance of reversing trends in declining ODA; further
strengthening complementary forms of development cooperation, including South -
South and triangular cooperation; and optimizing multilateral development bank
financing. It elevates country ownership and leadership alongside policy coherence
among core effectiveness principles and puts forward actions to put such principles
into practice, reducing fragmentation, enhancing coordination of all relevant actors
and strengthening alignment with country plans and needs. At the global level, the
Sevilla Commitment supports the United Nations in playing a central and
coordinating role in development cooperation and recognizes the need for in clusive
multilateral dialogue on parameters and objectives of international development
cooperation. It also strengthens the mandate of the Development Cooperation Forum
to foster synergies across existing platforms and forums, deepen dialogue among all
relevant actors, and enhance coherence and impact of development cooperation.

23. Development partners need to collectively intensify their efforts to meet the
ambition of the Sevilla Commitment on international development cooperation.
Ongoing reforms across multilateral development banks are unlocking additional
financing capacity and strengthening collaboration across multilateral development

lending, with a view to tripling it in the medium term. The use of special drawing
rights for the acquisition of hybrid capital instruments by multilateral development
banks remains a technically viable and promising pathway to this end and countries

D. International trade as an engine for development

27. The Sevilla Commitment recognizes the role of international trade as an engine
for inclusive growth and poverty eradication and highlights its contributions to
promoting sustainable development. It also underlines the ongoing challenges facing
the multilateral trading system, including a rise in trade restrictions and stall ing
multilateral negotiations to reform the system. Structural challenges constrain a large
number of developing countries with limited productive capacities in integrating their
firms in regional and global value chains.

28. The Sevilla Commitment proposes concrete actions to strengthen trade
capacities of developing countries, boost trade in the least developed countries, and
to increase local value addition and beneficiation of critical minerals and commodities
for economic diversification in developing countries. However, the conflict in the
Middle East, disruptions to global trade and rising uncertainties have curtailed efforts
by Member States and the international community to implement these actions at the
national and global levels.

29. In the past year, global trade has been directly affected by increasing tensions
and geopolitical risks, with the conflict in the Middle East the latest illustration of the
impact of instability on international trade. Trade trends are pointing downward, with
estimates suggesting that merchandise trade growth will decelerate from about 4.7 per
cent in 2025 to between 1.5 and 2.5 per cent in 2026, with significant impacts on
developing countries, particularly in Asia and Africa.11 Disruptions around the Strait
of Hormuz created a massive supply shock in essential trade flows: the week prior to
the conflict, 38 per cent of crude oil, 19 per cent of liquefied natural gas and 13 per
cent of chemicals, including fertilizers, passed through the Strait of Hormuz.12 Daily
ship traffic has dropped by 95 per cent, from around 100 to 130 ships a day in February
2026 to an average of less than 20 ships per day between 1 March and 14 June.13

30. Developing countries, particularly those in special situations, have the least
capacity to mitigate the effects of shocks in a fragmented global trading system.
Countries that are net oil importers, which include 86 per cent of least developed
countries and 87 per cent of small island developing States, are particularly
vulnerable. Estimates suggest that these vulnerable countries face a rise in oil import
costs of up to $20 billion a year.14 Second order effects through inflationary and
exchange rate pressures, as well as worsening debt sustainability burdens are
weighing on countries’ policy space to pursue economic diversification, strengthen
trade capacities and invest in trade-related infrastructures. In addition to the impact
of the conflict, the rise of tariffs have hit least developed countries particularly hard.

31. At the same time, the rapid rise in South-South trade and the growing demand
for digital services and environmental goods offer new opportunities. The value of
South-South trade has risen more than 4-fold in the past 20 years. 15 The higher
technology intensity of South-South trade compared to North-South trade signals that
there is potential to foster economic diversification and build trading capacity in
digital and trade sectors. Between 2014 and 2024, digitally deliverable ser vices grew
