E. Debt and debt sustainability

32. In the Sevilla Commitment a comprehensive package of international and
country-level actions is set out to address sovereign debt challenges faced by
developing countries and advance a more development-oriented debt architecture. It
focuses on four pillars: (i) preventing debt crises through strengthened debt
management, improved debt transparency and responsible borrowing and lending;
(ii) lowering borrowing costs and providing more comprehensive and systematic
support for developing countries that, while solvent, face high debt servicing costs;
(iii) reforming the global debt architecture to enable more timely, orderly, effective,
fair, predictable and coordinated debt restructurings; and (iv) enhancing debt
sustainability and credit assessments to ensure they are accurate, objective and long -
term oriented.

33. Global financing conditions have tightened over the past year, exacerbating debt
challenges in developing countries. Many developing countries already faced
elevated fiscal pressures driven by high external and domestic debt servicing, limiting
their capacity to respond to new shocks. Although debt levels had stabilized in 2024
and 2025, following COVID-19 pandemic-driven increases, they remain above
pre-pandemic levels, with debt service burdens at levels comparable to those in the
early 2000s. External debt interest payments by low- and middle-income countries
more than doubled over the past decade, reaching $415 billion in 2024, a new record
for the second year in a row. Bond yields have increased as a result of the ongoing
conflict, though with differentiated impacts across countries. Market access countries
face elevated refinancing costs and exchange rate pressures, amplifying their debt
service burdens. least developed countries are facing compounded shocks from trade
disruptions, higher food and energy prices and declining official development
assistance, further constricting fiscal space.

34. Despite the challenging context, the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment
debt package has advanced across the four pillars. Work is under way to
operationalize the Working Group on Principles of Responsible Borrowing and
Lending, aimed at establishing a coherent framework on borrower and lender
responsibilities. The Borrowers’ Platform, launched on the sidelines of the 2026
International Monetary Fund-World Bank Spring Meetings, provides a dedicated
forum for debtor countries to discuss technical issues, share experiences and
strengthen borrower countries’ voices in the global debt architecture.

35. Efforts to enhance debt transparency and improve reporting are progressing. The
World Bank is advancing the development of a global central debt data registry,
building upon improvements to its Debtor Reporting System and an annual debt
reconciliation process currently conducted with Group of 7 and Paris Club creditors,
with plans to expand coverage to all Group of 20 creditors. Uptake of debt pause
clauses has expanded among bilateral and multilateral creditors, with the Spain -led
Debt Pause Clause Alliance continuing to drive momentum in this area. A recent
proposal by the London Coalition on Sustainable Sovereign Debt to extend such

debtor countries and non-bonded commercial creditors.

F. International financial architecture and systemic issues

42. The Sevilla Commitment lays out an ambitious package of actions to address
international financial architecture challenges for a more crisis-prone world, across
five pillars: (i) strengthening global economic governance; (ii) strengthening the
global financial safety net; (iii) promoting long-term credit ratings; (iv) enhancing
financial regulation; (v) reaping potential benefits and considering macroeconomic
risks arising from new technologies in international payment.

43. There has so far not been any significant progress on governance reforms, which
have become more difficult to advance in the current geopolitical context and amid
growing fragmentation. At the April 2026 meetings, IMF Governors agreed to a set
of new guiding principles for governance reform and to develop a new IMF quota
formula, but did not set a new timeline for formula revisions nor address the many
missed past deadlines. The end-2023 outcome of the sixteenth IMF general review of
quotas, to increase the IMF quotas by 50 per cent, has still not been implemented
because of insufficient number of formal consents to the quota increase. At the World
Bank, the Executive Board concluded the 2025 shareholding review n oting there is
not sufficient support to issue new shares which would rebalance voting rights but
did endorse a proposal for enhancing client voice. Similarly, prospects for reforms to
IMF lending policies remain uncertain. There are also currently no plans referenced
in the IMF Executive Board work programme for the creation of a playbook, as called
for in the Sevilla Commitment.

44. More frequent economic and other shocks are expected to increase demands
placed on the global financial safety net – not only in relation to its size and coverage,
but also in how predictably, rapidly and affordably countries can access its resources.
Many developing countries are both more exposed to and more likely to lack
sufficient economic buffers to absorb shocks, with growing demand on the institutions
of the global financial safety net likely. These demands and the evolution of global
financial safety net are influenced in part by geopolitics: for instance, the United

States of America recently signalled that currency swap lines could be promoted to
reinforce global dollar dominance and secure geopolitical alignments with countries
in the Gulf or Asia. 19 Strengthening all layers of the global financial safety net,
including regional arrangements such as the proposed African Financing Stability
Mechanism, is essential to enhance the resilience of countries to external shocks.
Financing mechanisms should increasingly rely on pre-arranged instruments,
including insurance and contingency financing, that can be activated rapidly when
crises materialize. The Financing for shock-driven food crises from the Food and
Agriculture Organization of the United Nations is one example of a financing facility
that aims to anticipate, prevent and respond to escalating food emergencies before
they become unmanageable.

45. On financial regulation, the Sevilla Commitment invites further research on the
impact of risk-weighting frameworks and prudential standards on financing for
developing countries, while encouraging consideration of transition plans and climate
stress testing in regulatory frameworks. These efforts are being supported through a
dedicated high-impact initiative under the Sevilla Platform for Action which focuses
on regulatory barriers to investment in developing countries. Since its launch at
financing for development in Sevilla, a 4P Eminent Persons Group has held several
high-level meetings, notably during the General Assembly high-level week in
September 2025, with a particular focus on possible unintended effects of prudential
rules for banks and insurance companies.

G. Science, technology, innovation and capacity-building

46. In the Sevilla Commitment the role of science, technology and innovation in
advancing sustainable development is recognized, while acknowledging that the
ability of developing countries to leverage their full potential remains constrained.
The unintended economic, environmental and social consequences of technological
advances, including risks of widening gender inequality and the exclusion of
vulnerable groups, are also noted. The Sevilla Commitment calls for realizing the
potential of digital financial services to advance financial inclusion and health. Its
implementation is proceeding through national and international actions, including
wider adoption of national digital and innovation strategies, new mechanisms to
advance global artificial intelligence governance, joint United Nations and
multilateral development banks efforts to mobilize digital infrastructure investment
and the rapid expansion of digital financial services.

47. The conflict in the Middle East has exposed the physical vulnerabilities
underpinning the digital economy and artificial intelligence. Disruptions to energy
and critical materials supplies, transiting the Strait of Hormuz, have raised electricity
costs and tightened markets for inputs essential to semiconductor manufacturing.
Data centres have been directly targeted in the conflict, prompting a repricing of
geopolitical risk that may divert artificial intelligence infrastructure investment
towards jurisdictions offering greater security and away from developing regions
seeking to build capacity. These dynamics compound existing constraints: developing
countries face higher financing costs for digital infrastructure, narrower fiscal space
for science, technology and innovation investment and a heightened risk that the
artificial intelligence and digital divides widen as computing power, energy and
capital concentrate among a small number of economies.

48. Nonetheless, many of the actions agreed in the Sevilla Commitment science,
technology and innovation package are advanced in leveraging technologies for
sustainable development, digital infrastructure and digital public goods and digital

financial services, building upon ongoing progress. By 2024, 86 per cent of
developing countries had adopted national digital strategies, up from fewer than half

Mission-oriented innovation policy is expanding, with OECD identifying 241 active

Persistent skills gaps reinforce digital divides, with only 4 per cent of the population

49. Artificial intelligence innovation and investment have accelerated sharply but
are highly concentrated, deepening the risk of an artificial intelligence divide. Global
venture capital investment in artificial intelligence firms rose from about $8.4 billion
in 2012 to $258.7 billion in 2025, with the United States accounting for three quarters
of the latest-year total.21 Public policy readiness is advancing in parallel: the first
session of the United Nations Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance,
held in July 2026, addressed the development implications of artificial intelligence,
the artificial intelligence divide, international cooperation and human oversight. The
preliminary report of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel
on Artificial Intelligence identifies insufficient scientific evidence as a crucial
challenge, urging stronger country capacity to act on evidence of artificial intelligence
impacts.

50. International cooperation, connectivity and digital finance show progress
alongside persistent gaps. Scientific collaboration has lost momentum since 2019,
while 74 per cent of the global population was online in 2025, yet only 23 per cent in
low-income countries, against a digital infrastructure financing gap of $1.5 trillion to
$1.7 trillion through 2030. Under the Sevilla Platform for Action, the International
Telecommunication Union and United Nations Conference on Trade and
Development (UNCTAD), and eight multilateral development banks, launched the
Digital Infrastructure Investment Catalyser to close this gap. Digital financial services
are expanding rapidly: mobile money use among adults in developing countries rose
from 3 per cent a decade ago to 32 per cent in 2024, and global financial technology
(fintech) investment rebounded to $116 billion in 2025, up from a seven -year low of
$95.5 billion in 2024. However, growing spillovers from fintech, including
stablecoins, potentially reaching $2 trillion by 2028, pose financial stability risks.22

Data, monitoring and follow-up

51. Timely, reliable, high-quality and disaggregated data and statistics are essential
for advancing the financing for development agenda, which was recognized in the
Sevilla Commitment. It commits to supporting developing countries in enhancing
investment in data and statistical systems and to strengthen the interoperability of
data and statistical frameworks for sustainable development. The Sevilla
Commitment also takes important steps to strengthen the follow -up to the Financing
for Development outcomes, at the national, regional and global levels. Notable
progress demonstrated by strengthened data systems and infrastru cture, expanded
Sustainable Development Goal indicator coverage and advances in South -South
cooperation reporting is threatened by declining external financing, especially in low -
income countries.

52. The availability and quality of data for monitoring the Sustainable Development
Goals have improved substantially. Nearly 70 per cent of indicators have good
coverage and all 234 indicators have well-established methodologies to date. The
Global Sustainable Development Goal Indicators Database expanded to 3.3 million
data records by October 2025, up from 1.4 million in 2020. 23 Nonetheless, gaps
persist in disaggregated data, especially on cross-cutting dimensions, such as gender,
disability and income.

53. Despite low global progress in statistical performance, many lower-income
countries improved due to strengthened data infrastructure. However, declining
external financing from 2024 onward poses a significant risk. The fall in ODA is
likely to affect funding for data and statistics, which generally follows overall ODA
funding trends, disproportionately affecting low-income countries. Major
international programmes that support household level data collection in developing
countries have experienced cuts in their funding. Notably, the abrupt termination of
substantial funding for the Demographic and Health Surveys could severally impact
health and gender data infrastructure in developing countries. The Financing for
Development and the Future of Data, a Sevilla Platform for Action initiative, is
advancing efficient data financing, future-proofing data investment and strengthening
political commitment and cross‑sector coordination.

54. Integrated data systems and open platforms enhance accessibility and use of
data and information by decision makers across sectors. The coordinated development
of the System of National Accounts 2025 and Balance of Payments and International
Investment Position Manual (seventh edition) demonstrates the benefits of strategic
coordinated approaches to developing modern, coherent and efficient international
standards.

55. Progress has been achieved in South-South cooperation data reporting. In 2026,
nine pilot countries in Latin American and the Caribbean reported initial data using
the United Nations framework to measure South-South cooperation. Scholarships and
humanitarian assistance are the leading modalities, followed by monetary
contributions to infrastructure projects and technical cooperation. Complementary
initiatives can play a vital role in expanding these efforts. The South -South Data
Fund, created in 2025, aims to support countries to measure and report on their South-
South cooperation flows. As at March 2026, 66 developing economies have requested
immediate support. A community of practice to leverage South -South data, a Sevilla
Platform for Action initiative, also provides a platform for peer support and technical
sharing among countries.

56. The work to develop a framework of measures beyond GDP is progressing. The
Secretary-General’s independent High-level Expert Group on Beyond GDP presented
its final report on 7 May 2026, with concrete recommendations, including a
conceptual framework; an indicator dashboard; and recommendations on how to
implement this agenda. As a next step, Member States will initiate an
intergovernmental progress to consider the recommendations of the Expert Group.
This will include considering the use of the beyond GDP framework in financing
policy frameworks, e.g. allocation rules for concessional finance.

57. The Sevilla Commitment encourages the appointment of national focal points
for financing for development in finance and other relevant ministries, while General
Assembly resolution 80/129 invited the Secretariat to facilitate the establishment of
a network of voluntary national focal points for financing for development. After a
call for nominations, the Network of National Focal Points on Financing for
Development was officially launched at a high-level event in April. National focal
points convened for three dedicated sessions to operationalize the network, defining
possible working modalities and translating its core objectives – peer-to-peer learning
and bridging national action with global financing for development commitments –
into practical implementation plans. As of June 2026, the Secretariat had received
nominations of 169 individuals from 87 Member States to serve as national focal
points. Almost 100 of the individuals are from finance ministries. A survey of focal
points conducted in May and June will inform plans for engagements and briefings
during the eighty-first session of the General Assembly. National focal points will
reconvene in a hybrid format at the 2027 financing for development forum.

58. The 2026 ECOSOC forum on financing for development follow -up, held from
20 to 24 April 2026, marked the first major intergovernmental stocktaking of progress
in implementing the Sevilla Commitment. It reviewed advances and gaps across all
seven action areas and highlighted priorities for implementation. The Forum also
helped operationalize the strengthened follow-up architecture agreed in Sevilla, with
in-depth reviews of domestic and international private business and finance;
international trade as an engine for development; international financial architecture
and systemic issues; and data, monitoring and follow-up and separate special high-
level meetings with the Bretton Woods institutions and with the World Trade
Organization and UNCTAD. The Forum’s intergovernmentally agreed outcome
(E/FFDF/2026/3), adopted by consensus, sent a positive signal for multilateral
cooperation at a challenging moment, recorded actions already under way and
provided guidance on areas where near-term action should be concentrated.

III. Conclusions

59. Implementation efforts are proceeding across all action areas of the Financing
for Development outcomes. In several areas, initiatives of the Sevilla Platform for
Action contribute to implementation momentum and tangible progress. But the
overall picture is concerning. Major aspects of international financial architecture
reform, in particular those related to governance, are stalled, in a geopolitically
fraught environment. In some critical areas, not least the provision of concessional
financing and ODA, there is dramatic regression. The global macroeconomic and
geopolitical environment remains extraordinarily challenging, exacerbating a
financing squeeze for the poorest and most vulnerable countries.

60. In light of the holistic nature of the financing for development agenda, these
setbacks threaten to undermine progress across all action areas. Full and timely
implementation of the Sevilla Commitment thus remains critical. The most recent
global shock underlines the need to strengthen investment in resilience and capacity
for crisis response in particular.

A/81/336
26-1202316/16

61. Countries should undertake steps to sustainably mobilize resources domestically
and developed countries should make every effort to not only protect support to
developing countries to strengthen domestic revenue mobilization from cuts, but to
scale it up to collectively at least double it by 2030, in line with the Sevilla
Commitment. All countries should continue efforts to better align their fiscal systems
with sustainable development; for example, the current disruptions to energy supplies
underline the value of windfall taxes that can help make fiscal systems more resilient
against shocks.

62. Rising volatility in global markets and the uneven recovery in international
financing flows have also underlined the importance of countries building robust and
resilient domestic financial systems. Countries should prioritize the building of a
strong domestic savings base and a resilient domestic banking system that is geared
towards mobilizing local savings and unlocking investment in the local economy.
International support and measures to increase the availability of financing in local
currency can have a catalytic effect for building and deepening domestic financial
markets.

63. By expanding their lending during crises, multilateral development banks make
important contributions to the core layers of the global financial safety net. They are
demonstrating this ability in the current crisis and should consider further scaling up
pre-arranged financing modalities to facilitate timely support. At the same time, the
multilateral development banks and their shareholders should also develop concrete
road maps towards fulfilling the ambition of the Sevilla Commitment to potentially
triple their lending capacity.

64. Sovereign debt challenges remain a major stumbling block to financing the
Sustainable Development Goal investments at scale. The progress on mainstreaming
debt pause clauses in official and commercial lending is welcome; stakeholders
should pursue scalable and standardized approaches, with broad triggers capable of
responding to a wide range of shocks, such as those recently proposed by the London
Coalition on Sustainable Sovereign Debt. At the same time, high debt service burdens
continue to greatly constrain fiscal space, underlining the need for scaling up support
in this area, e.g. by operationalizing the support on debt and liquidity management
envisaged in the Sevilla Commitment. Complex and slow restructuring processes may
have contributed to some highly indebted countries engaging in complex and
sometimes opaque transactions that will further test the restructuring architecture.
Member States should create and make use of inclusive spaces, such as the dialogue
on debt mandated in the Sevilla Commitment, to identify gaps and proposals for
closing gaps in the debt architecture.

65. Efforts are also needed to make the global financial safety net more responsive
to shocks and emerging risks, with greater emphasis on early action, predictability,
flexibility and effective coordination across institutions. The global financial safety
net should be capable not only of mobilizing resources at scale, but also of delivering
support rapidly, predictably, and coherently. Financing mechanisms should
increasingly rely on pre-arranged instruments, including insurance and contingency
financing, that can be activated rapidly when crises materialize. Early warning
systems, real-time data and advanced forecasting tools can help identify risks before
they escalate, allowing institutions to disburse emergency funding more quickly and
effectively.

paragraphs.text: In its resolution 80/129, the General Assembly requested the Secretary-General to submit a report to the Assembly at its eighty-first session on the follow-up to and the implementation of the Financing for Development outcomes and the Sevilla Commitment, including on progress made and continuing challenges faced.

In the context of growing volatility, more frequent and extreme shocks and geoeconomic fragmentation, the present report presents progress and challenges in the implementation of the Financing for Development outcomes, with particular emphasis on the effects of crises on the financing agenda and on possible financing policy responses, at both the national and international levels.

The Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development took place in a challenging context, characterized by rising trade and geopolitical tensions, more frequent and intense climate shocks and a difficult macroeconomic environment. Developing countries, particularly the poorest and most vulnerable, are facing a financing squeeze; in a period of tepid global growth, progress on mobilizing additional domestic resources has been limited, with convergence between developing and developed countries stalling after the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic; foreign direct investment showed resilience in 2025, but increased by only 2 per cent in developing countries, after falls in earlier years; a sharp drop in official development assistance (ODA), trade turbulence, high costs of capital and historically high debt service burdens further add to financing challenges. 1

These challenges have been exacerbated by a series of shocks in recent years. These shocks have had significant macroeconomic and financing repercussions, often affecting countries in a highly uneven manner. The conflict in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is only the latest such example, with impacts determined by countries’ exposure to its core transmission channels (energy markets, fertilizers and other supply chains and financial flows) and their capacity to respond. Many energy-importing developing economies face new growth headwinds, inflationary pressures and balance-of-payments strains. While countries in Asia are most exposed to the energy shock, countries in Africa and least developed countries are highly vulnerable to rising food prices and also have the least capacity to implement macroeconomic responses, in view of limited fiscal space or external buffers. Depending on the length of the conflict, its spillovers could become much more damaging, testing the institutions providing the global financial safety net.2

The Sevilla Commitment renewed the global framework for financing for development and updated the agenda to make it fit for purpose for a more crisis-prone world. It contains commitments to address the financing squeeze and debt sustainability pressures, increase financial flows and investment in sustainable development and the Sustainable Development Goals, strengthen countries’ resilience and make the international financial architecture better equipped to support countries in addressing current challenges and absorbing future shocks. This includes stepping up investment in crisis prevention and resilience, scaling up pre -arranged financing and instruments that provide automatic breathing space during shocks and strengthening the global financial safety net, among other actions.

The financing for development agenda is holistic, with policies across all action areas required to sustainably and significantly increase financing and investment. It also balances actions at the domestic and international levels: country leadership is a key cross-cutting principle, while the international community is responsible for creating an enabling international economic environment. The Sevilla Commitment includes a strong package of actions on reform of the international financial, debt and development cooperation architectures, but also includes steps to strengthen national leadership in implementation, for example, by placing integrated national financing frameworks at the centre of efforts and by encouraging countries to appoint national focal points for financing for development.

The implementation of the Sevilla Commitment is taken forward by a wide range of actors. Some actions require global action and multilateral agreement or are taken forward within the United Nations, while others can be taken forward by coalitions of stakeholders. The Sevilla Platform for Action hosts 130 such coalitions, which have been directly supporting the implementation of 170 actions.

The Sevilla Commitment also strengthened the financing for development follow-up process; this report supports this follow-up by providing an assessment of progress made and challenges in its implementation, in each of the action areas. It puts emphasis on how external shocks and the existing gaps in the international financial architecture have impacted this implementation and makes recommendations on how the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment can help address these.

In the Sevilla Commitment it is recognized that mobilizing and effectively using domestic resources is a cornerstone of national ownership, long -term resilience and funding of public goods. An integrated reform agenda is set out in order to enhance fiscal systems, improve international tax cooperation, combat illicit financial flows and strengthen the role of national development banks.

The conflict in the Middle East, however, has compounded existing pressures on domestic public resources, particularly in non-oil-producing countries. Declining growth rates and disrupted trade flows are eroding tax bases. Many Governments have cut fuel taxes and introduced or expanded subsidies to protect households from rising inflationary pressures. According to an International Energy Agency policy response tracker, as at early June 2026, 54 countries had lowered energy taxes while 31 countries had increased fuel subsidies.3 For the most vulnerable countries, including least developed countries, constrained fiscal space risks limiting their capacity to finance the Sustainable Development Goals precisely when needs are most acute. On the other hand, some net exporting countries may also experience temporary gains from higher oil, natural gas or fertilizer prices. In such cases, the resulting windfall revenues should be managed prudently. Oil companies are expected to reap windfall profits, which can be taxed. Experience from 2022 shows that such windfall taxes can generate revenues without raising consumer prices, thus supporting the rebuilding of fiscal buffers, strengthening macroeconomic stability and mobilizing resources.

Structural tax capacity challenges long predate the current conflict. Although tax revenues have increased over time in both developed and developing countries, large gaps persist: by 2024, the median tax-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio in developed countries stood approximately 10 percentage points above that of developing countries. Some narrowing occurred between 2017 and 2020, but convergence stalled after the COVID-19 pandemic through uneven recovery paths. Today, 76 countries collect tax revenues below the 15 per cent of GDP threshold set in the Sevilla Commitment as a minimum floor.4

Advancing domestic public resources mobilization will require sustained domestic efforts alongside scaled-up international support, through demand-driven capacity-building, technical assistance and effective cooperation to counter tax avoidance and illicit flows. Prior to the most recent cuts in ODA, support for domestic revenue mobilization had grown but remained modest at $1.12 billion in 2024. 5 In the Sevilla Commitment, development partners were called upon to double their support in this area by 2030. While data to assess the implementation of this commitment is not yet available, scaled-up capacity support is the focus of 33 voluntary initiatives in this action area under the Sevilla Platform for Action.

There has been some concrete progress in the areas of international tax cooperation and combating of illicit financial flows. Member States have engaged constructively in negotiations on the United Nations framework convention on international tax cooperation, working on zero drafts ahead of the fifth session in August 2026. The Economic and Social Council convened its first -ever special meeting on financial integrity at United Nations Headquarters in New York on 4 February 2026, with a focus on two linked themes: (i) strengthening global coordination on policy and norm-setting for exchange of information and data; and (ii) enhancing enforcement capacities and innovation on the use of information and data. The meeting fostered dialogue among Member States and a broad range of intergovernmental bodies and stakeholders working across tax cooperation, anti-money-laundering and anti-corruption frameworks. Participants called for addressing structural asymmetries in access to information, prioritizing enhancing interoperability of data systems, promoting whole-of-government approaches at the national level and supporting integrated capacity development.

In the Sevilla Commitment a strong emphasis was placed on the role of public development banks, as a key lever to mobilize affordable long-term financing. In this context, it commits to several actions to realize the full potential of national public development banks. Such public development banks are widespread, but their footprint varies greatly. While present in a majority of countries, vulnerable countries, such as the least developed countries and small island developing States have lowest coverage, with only around two thirds of them having a national public development bank .

Private business activity, investment and innovation are important drivers of sustainable development. Nonetheless, global investment growth remains uneven and concentrated in a small number of countries and sectors, particularly in key technology sectors, such as artificial intelligence. Despite increased attention to innovative finance instruments, such as blended finance and some growing adoption of sustainable business and finance legislation, investment in sustainable development has fallen short of expectations.

Increased geopolitical uncertainty has affected private sector activity and affected the outlook for foreign direct investment, as some companies have postponed or cancelled specific projects. Micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises are particularly vulnerable to related price shocks as they are less able to absorb rising operational costs due to smaller margins and lower reserves. Countries with large migrant workforce present in countries affected by conflict have also witnessed falling inflows in remittances due to a downturn in labour markets in the workers’ host countries.

In this challenging context, the Sevilla Commitment includes commitments to address key barriers to greater private investment in the Sustainable Development Goals. First, underdeveloped financial and capital markets in many developing countries which contribute to insufficient access to finance, particularly for women, marginalized groups and micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises; and second, the continued misalignment between short-term financial incentives and long-term sustainable development impact, as well as the high cost of foreign exchange hedging, which call for a new approach to private capital mobilization.

Domestic efforts to implement the Sevilla Commitment are advancing against the backdrop of rising uncertainties in the global economy. Domestic financial markets in many developing countries face heightened risks related to rising debt sustainability challenges, increased market volatility and currency and capital outflow pressures. To tackle these vulnerabilities, countries should intensify efforts to build robust domestic financial markets, prioritizing the building of a strong domestic savings base and domestic and local banking sectors, before introducing more complex financial markets and instruments that risk being illiquid, underutilized and more prone to external shocks. Efforts should focus on strengthening the micro -, small and medium-sized enterprises ecosystem, particularly local, savings and cooperative banks, as well as national development banks, which play a critical role in unlocking lending for micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises in local currency. Complementary actions to facilitate lending in local currencies, including efforts by multilateral development banks and other public development banks to build a shared pool of local currencies that reduces the cost of hedging, can support such efforts. The reversal in remittance flows due to the conflict in the Middle East has also put a renewed spotlight on efforts to reduce the cost of remittances.

Regarding private capital mobilization, blended finance continues to grow in importance but remains below expectations and concentrated in specific countries and sectors, largely bypassing countries most in need. Over the period from 2015 to 2024, private finance mobilized through blended finance grew from $32 billion to $75 billion.6 Volumes mobilized were four times higher in middle-income countries than in the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States combined.7 Several initiatives under the Sevilla Platform for Action have begun to tackle these issues. They are showing early results in capital mobilization through tailored solutions, including foreign exchange hedging, insurance, grants and technical assistance. An increased focus on alignment with country priorities, more effective design and use of instruments, increased collaboration across the blended finance ecosystem and improved data can lead to scaled-up private capital mobilization and greater impact.

Sustainable finance continues to mature as a field, gaining grounds in some major developing markets – especially across the Asia-Pacific region – even as it faces backlash in others. Yet, gaps remain that require both innovative mechanisms to realign private incentives with sustainable development – such as blended finance structures or thematic bonds that ring-fence capital for specific development outcomes – as well as clearer regulatory direction through policy tools like taxonomies and disclosure requirements, alongside greater interoperability across standards and jurisdictions. The Sevilla Platform for Action initiative in paragraph 34 brings together standard-setters and United Nations system agencies under a single coordinated umbrella to help advance these efforts within the financing for development agenda.

The Sevilla Commitment recognizes the significant contribution of international development cooperation to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while acknowledging that it has not kept pace with rising and evolving needs of developing countries. Amid mutually reinforcing global challenges and increasingly frequent shocks, demands on international development cooperation are rising, while available resources, including ODA, are declining, with fewer resources reaching developing countries. In 2025, ODA provided by member and associates of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Development Assistance Committee fell by 23.1 per cent in real terms compared with 2024, to $174.3 billion, representing the largest annual drop in the history of ODA. These cuts occurred after a 7.1 per cent fall in 2024 and are projected to be followed by a further decline in ODA of 6 per cent in 2026, despite growing needs. 8 This historic fall in ODA is disproportionately affecting the poorest countries, where ODA remains macrocritical. In least developed countries, where bilateral ODA represents on average 15 per cent of Government revenues, ODA fell by 25.8 per cent in 2025, with direct impacts on their ability to finance their sustainable development.

The Sevilla Commitment includes a series of actions to help to bridge the gap between falling supply and rising demand for international development cooperation: emphasizing the importance of reversing trends in declining ODA; further strengthening complementary forms of development cooperation, including South - South and triangular cooperation; and optimizing multilateral development bank financing. It elevates country ownership and leadership alongside policy coherence among core effectiveness principles and puts forward actions to put such principles into practice, reducing fragmentation, enhancing coordination of all relevant actors and strengthening alignment with country plans and needs. At the global level, the Sevilla Commitment supports the United Nations in playing a central and coordinating role in development cooperation and recognizes the need for in clusive multilateral dialogue on parameters and objectives of international development cooperation. It also strengthens the mandate of the Development Cooperation Forum to foster synergies across existing platforms and forums, deepen dialogue among all relevant actors, and enhance coherence and impact of development cooperation.

Development partners need to collectively intensify their efforts to meet the ambition of the Sevilla Commitment on international development cooperation. Ongoing reforms across multilateral development banks are unlocking additional financing capacity and strengthening collaboration across multilateral development banks and other public development banks; though there is scope to further scale up lending, with a view to tripling it in the medium term. The use of special drawing rights for the acquisition of hybrid capital instruments by multilateral development banks remains a technically viable and promising pathway to this end and countries in a position to do so should contribute to the solution developed by the African Development Bank and Inter-American Development Bank.

Building on the Group of 20 Capital Adequacy Framework review and the Group of 20 road map towards better, bigger and more effective multilateral development banks, ongoing reform efforts across multilateral development banks are contributing to unlocking additional financing capacity. In 2025, multilateral development banks reported that the full implementation of agreed reform measures could generate more than $600 billion in new lending capacity. Closer engagement between multilateral development banks and credit rating agencies has added further momentum: after incorporating the multilateral development bank -driven Global Emerging Markets database into its assessment of multilateral development bank portfolio risk and capital requirements, S&P Global estimated that multilateral development banks have an additional $600 to $800 billion in lending capacity that could be deployed in the next decade without putting their ratings at risk. 9 At the country level, against a backdrop of growing fragmentation, there is room to strengthen development partners’ alignment with country plans and results frameworks, increase the use of national systems and improve the timeliness and predictability of development cooperation information. Developing countries are putting in place plans and strategies, but participation of development partners needs to be strengthened. Progress on policy coherence, including untying aid, is mixed. While tied aid has decreased as a share of total bilateral aid, almost half of the total value of untied contracts funded by Development Assistance Committee members was awarded to suppliers from their countries and only 40 per cent to suppliers from developing countries.10

At the global level, several initiatives have emerged to reimagine development cooperation amid shifting political priorities. Some of these were launched under the Sevilla Platform for Action and are reporting progress in building coalitions and securing political commitment. The OECD Development Assistance Committee review process has also been advancing, with the view of reviewing and improving its role, tools and partnerships. The Development Cooperation Forum in 2027 will provide a space for updates and exchanges among all Member States on identified priorities and emerging recommendations from such initiatives and discussions on the way forward.

The Baku to Belém Roadmap published in advance of the thirtieth session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change charted a pathway to further scale up climate finance and deliver on the decision adopted at the twenty-ninth session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change through a series of dedicated actions by all actors working together in the short and medium term to strengthen leadership and accountability. Climate finance provided and mobilized by developed countries totalled $136.7 billion in 2024, exceeding the previous $100 billion annual goal. Alongside efforts to increase volumes of climate finance, data quality and reporting need to be strengthened to ensure adequate tracking of progress towards agreed goals. Development finance for preserving biodiversity, for combating desertification, land degradation and drought, and for a sustainable ocean economy is also not keeping pace with needs.

The Sevilla Commitment recognizes the role of international trade as an engine for inclusive growth and poverty eradication and highlights its contributions to promoting sustainable development. It also underlines the ongoing challenges facing the multilateral trading system, including a rise in trade restrictions and stall ing multilateral negotiations to reform the system. Structural challenges constrain a large number of developing countries with limited productive capacities in integrating their firms in regional and global value chains.

The Sevilla Commitment proposes concrete actions to strengthen trade capacities of developing countries, boost trade in the least developed countries, and to increase local value addition and beneficiation of critical minerals and commodities for economic diversification in developing countries. However, the conflict in the Middle East, disruptions to global trade and rising uncertainties have curtailed efforts by Member States and the international community to implement these actions at the national and global levels.

In the past year, global trade has been directly affected by increasing tensions and geopolitical risks, with the conflict in the Middle East the latest illustration of the impact of instability on international trade. Trade trends are pointing downward, with estimates suggesting that merchandise trade growth will decelerate from about 4.7 per cent in 2025 to between 1.5 and 2.5 per cent in 2026, with significant impacts on developing countries, particularly in Asia and Africa.11 Disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz created a massive supply shock in essential trade flows: the week prior to the conflict, 38 per cent of crude oil, 19 per cent of liquefied natural gas and 13 per cent of chemicals, including fertilizers, passed through the Strait of Hormuz.12 Daily ship traffic has dropped by 95 per cent, from around 100 to 130 ships a day in February 2026 to an average of less than 20 ships per day between 1 March and 14 June.13

Developing countries, particularly those in special situations, have the least capacity to mitigate the effects of shocks in a fragmented global trading system. Countries that are net oil importers, which include 86 per cent of least developed countries and 87 per cent of small island developing States, are particularly vulnerable. Estimates suggest that these vulnerable countries face a rise in oil import costs of up to $20 billion a year.14 Second order effects through inflationary and exchange rate pressures, as well as worsening debt sustainability burdens are weighing on countries’ policy space to pursue economic diversification, strengthen trade capacities and invest in trade-related infrastructures. In addition to the impact of the conflict, the rise of tariffs have hit least developed countries particularly hard.

At the same time, the rapid rise in South-South trade and the growing demand for digital services and environmental goods offer new opportunities. The value of South-South trade has risen more than 4-fold in the past 20 years. 15 The higher technology intensity of South-South trade compared to North-South trade signals that there is potential to foster economic diversification and build trading capacity in digital and trade sectors. Between 2014 and 2024, digitally deliverable ser vices grew by 6.8 per cent annually, faster than total service exports. 16 Nonetheless, while digitally deliverable services represented 61 per cent of services exports in developed economies, they represented only 16 per cent in least developed countries, underscoring a huge digital divide. Strengthening the capacities of countries to take advantage of these opportunities, including those relating to the low -carbon and digital transformations, will be critical.

In the Sevilla Commitment a comprehensive package of international and country-level actions is set out to address sovereign debt challenges faced by developing countries and advance a more development-oriented debt architecture. It focuses on four pillars: (i) preventing debt crises through strengthened debt management, improved debt transparency and responsible borrowing and lending; (ii) lowering borrowing costs and providing more comprehensive and systematic support for developing countries that, while solvent, face high debt servicing costs; (iii) reforming the global debt architecture to enable more timely, orderly, effective, fair, predictable and coordinated debt restructurings; and (iv) enhancing debt sustainability and credit assessments to ensure they are accurate, objective and long - term oriented.

Global financing conditions have tightened over the past year, exacerbating debt challenges in developing countries. Many developing countries already faced elevated fiscal pressures driven by high external and domestic debt servicing, limiting their capacity to respond to new shocks. Although debt levels had stabilized in 2024 and 2025, following COVID-19 pandemic-driven increases, they remain above pre-pandemic levels, with debt service burdens at levels comparable to those in the early 2000s. External debt interest payments by low- and middle-income countries more than doubled over the past decade, reaching $415 billion in 2024, a new record for the second year in a row. Bond yields have increased as a result of the ongoing conflict, though with differentiated impacts across countries. Market access countries face elevated refinancing costs and exchange rate pressures, amplifying their debt service burdens. least developed countries are facing compounded shocks from trade disruptions, higher food and energy prices and declining official development assistance, further constricting fiscal space.

Despite the challenging context, the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment debt package has advanced across the four pillars. Work is under way to operationalize the Working Group on Principles of Responsible Borrowing and Lending, aimed at establishing a coherent framework on borrower and lender responsibilities. The Borrowers’ Platform, launched on the sidelines of the 2026 International Monetary Fund-World Bank Spring Meetings, provides a dedicated forum for debtor countries to discuss technical issues, share experiences and strengthen borrower countries’ voices in the global debt architecture.

Efforts to enhance debt transparency and improve reporting are progressing. The World Bank is advancing the development of a global central debt data registry, building upon improvements to its Debtor Reporting System and an annual debt reconciliation process currently conducted with Group of 7 and Paris Club creditors, with plans to expand coverage to all Group of 20 creditors. Uptake of debt pause clauses has expanded among bilateral and multilateral creditors, with the Spain -led Debt Pause Clause Alliance continuing to drive momentum in this area. A recent proposal by the London Coalition on Sustainable Sovereign Debt to extend such clauses to bonded debt has received positive feedback from credit rating agencies, potentially catalysing broader private sector adoption.

There has been progress on actions in the Sevilla Commitment that aim to lower sovereign borrowing cost and provide more comprehensive and systematic liquidity support. The Small Island Developing States Debt Sustainability Support Service has been operationalized as part of the Small Island Developing States Centre of Excellence, established under the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States: A Renewed Declaration for Resilient Prosperity. The Debt Sustainability Support Service aims to provide support to small island developing States on strengthening debt sustainability, including through using debt swaps, resilience-investment financing, insurance tools and expert advisory services. To advance the implementation of the three-pillar approach to support countries faced with liquidity challenges, the International Monetary Fund and World Bank developed a manual to provide practical guidance to policymakers and debt managers on liability management operations supported by credit enhancements. The World Bank and Spain launched the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps to promote standardization, coordination and technical support. Despite these notable efforts, more support is required for developing countries facing high debt serv icing costs. The Sevilla Commitment called for a dedicated facility to offer coordinated and enhanced liquidity and debt management support at scale, which is yet to be implemented.

In terms of improvements to the debt architecture, the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable developed a restructuring playbook (updated in April 2026) that summarizes the key steps, concepts and processes in recent debt restructurings under the Group of 20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the Debt Service Suspension Initiative. Post-pandemic debt restructurings have shortened in the most recent cases: Ghana, the most recent country to conclude an external bond exchange under the Common Framework, did so in 1.9 years, compared with 4.1 years for the earlier case of Zambia.17 Nevertheless, restructurings remain longer than the typical time frame observed in the past. On average, external debt restructurings during the period 2020–2024 took approximately 2.5 years, compared with an average duration of just over one year between 2014 and 2020. 18 This reflects the increasing complexity in restructuring processes, driven by significant changes in the creditor landscape, with a growing share of non-traditional and private creditors that has complicated coordination, as well as more complex financing arrangements, such as the use of collateralized lending instruments. Most recently, several countries have reverted to total return swaps to secure short-term liquidity from international and regional banks, often using their own debt securities as collateral, raising concerns both around transparency and inter-creditor equity, which could complicate restructurings.

Delays in the restructuring of non-bonded commercial debt are generally attributed to the absence of an effective coordination mechanism. Recent efforts have sought to address these challenges and accelerate the restructuring process. The London Coalition has launched an implementation guide to restructuring private sector sovereign loans aimed at facilitating more efficient negotiations between the debtor countries and non-bonded commercial creditors.

Preparations are under way to convene a United Nations debt dialogue to provide an inclusive forum to bring together all stakeholders, including both borrowers and creditors, to assess trends in the debt landscape, review progress in architecture reforms and discuss gaps and challenges.

The ongoing review of the Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Framework by IMF and the World Bank aims to better reflect evolving debt dynamics, including the growing role of domestic debt, increasing instrument complexity and heightened exposure to global shocks. Key enhancements under consideration include the integration of a long-term climate module to more systematically capture climate- related risks and the macroeconomic benefits of climate investments.

There has also been some progress on credit ratings. ECOSOC convened the inaugural special high-level meeting on credit ratings on 30 March 2026, addressing the cost of capital, credit assessment methodologies and engagement between developing countries and credit rating agencies. Investors called for ratings to provide greater insight into the longer-term strategic intent of debt issuers- and major rating agencies confirmed they produce (or are working on producing) scenario and what -if analysis as a complement to base-case ratings, as called for in the Sevilla Commitment. Participants in the special meeting also affirmed that the ongoing review of the Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Framework could provide a useful benchmark for credit rating agencies to review their own methodologies. Participants also heard an update on efforts by African countries to create an Africa Credit Rating Agency.

The Sevilla Commitment lays out an ambitious package of actions to address international financial architecture challenges for a more crisis-prone world, across five pillars: (i) strengthening global economic governance; (ii) strengthening the global financial safety net; (iii) promoting long-term credit ratings; (iv) enhancing financial regulation; (v) reaping potential benefits and considering macroeconomic risks arising from new technologies in international payment.

There has so far not been any significant progress on governance reforms, which have become more difficult to advance in the current geopolitical context and amid growing fragmentation. At the April 2026 meetings, IMF Governors agreed to a set of new guiding principles for governance reform and to develop a new IMF quota formula, but did not set a new timeline for formula revisions nor address the many missed past deadlines. The end-2023 outcome of the sixteenth IMF general review of quotas, to increase the IMF quotas by 50 per cent, has still not been implemented because of insufficient number of formal consents to the quota increase. At the World Bank, the Executive Board concluded the 2025 shareholding review n oting there is not sufficient support to issue new shares which would rebalance voting rights but did endorse a proposal for enhancing client voice. Similarly, prospects for reforms to IMF lending policies remain uncertain. There are also currently no plans referenced in the IMF Executive Board work programme for the creation of a playbook, as called for in the Sevilla Commitment.

More frequent economic and other shocks are expected to increase demands placed on the global financial safety net – not only in relation to its size and coverage, but also in how predictably, rapidly and affordably countries can access its resources. Many developing countries are both more exposed to and more likely to lack sufficient economic buffers to absorb shocks, with growing demand on the institutions of the global financial safety net likely. These demands and the evolution of global financial safety net are influenced in part by geopolitics: for instance, the United States of America recently signalled that currency swap lines could be promoted to reinforce global dollar dominance and secure geopolitical alignments with countries in the Gulf or Asia. 19 Strengthening all layers of the global financial safety net, including regional arrangements such as the proposed African Financing Stability Mechanism, is essential to enhance the resilience of countries to external shocks. Financing mechanisms should increasingly rely on pre-arranged instruments, including insurance and contingency financing, that can be activated rapidly when crises materialize. The Financing for shock-driven food crises from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations is one example of a financing facility that aims to anticipate, prevent and respond to escalating food emergencies before they become unmanageable.

On financial regulation, the Sevilla Commitment invites further research on the impact of risk-weighting frameworks and prudential standards on financing for developing countries, while encouraging consideration of transition plans and climate stress testing in regulatory frameworks. These efforts are being supported through a dedicated high-impact initiative under the Sevilla Platform for Action which focuses on regulatory barriers to investment in developing countries. Since its launch at financing for development in Sevilla, a 4P Eminent Persons Group has held several high-level meetings, notably during the General Assembly high-level week in September 2025, with a particular focus on possible unintended effects of prudential rules for banks and insurance companies.

In the Sevilla Commitment the role of science, technology and innovation in advancing sustainable development is recognized, while acknowledging that the ability of developing countries to leverage their full potential remains constrained. The unintended economic, environmental and social consequences of technological advances, including risks of widening gender inequality and the exclusion of vulnerable groups, are also noted. The Sevilla Commitment calls for realizing the potential of digital financial services to advance financial inclusion and health. Its implementation is proceeding through national and international actions, including wider adoption of national digital and innovation strategies, new mechanisms to advance global artificial intelligence governance, joint United Nations and multilateral development banks efforts to mobilize digital infrastructure investment and the rapid expansion of digital financial services.

The conflict in the Middle East has exposed the physical vulnerabilities underpinning the digital economy and artificial intelligence. Disruptions to energy and critical materials supplies, transiting the Strait of Hormuz, have raised electricity costs and tightened markets for inputs essential to semiconductor manufacturing. Data centres have been directly targeted in the conflict, prompting a repricing of geopolitical risk that may divert artificial intelligence infrastructure investment towards jurisdictions offering greater security and away from developing regions seeking to build capacity. These dynamics compound existing constraints: developing countries face higher financing costs for digital infrastructure, narrower fiscal space for science, technology and innovation investment and a heightened risk that the artificial intelligence and digital divides widen as computing power, energy and capital concentrate among a small number of economies.

Nonetheless, many of the actions agreed in the Sevilla Commitment science, technology and innovation package are advanced in leveraging technologies for sustainable development, digital infrastructure and digital public goods and digital financial services, building upon ongoing progress. By 2024, 86 per cent of developing countries had adopted national digital strategies, up from fewer than half in 2017, though many still lack alignment with industrial and environmental policies. Mission-oriented innovation policy is expanding, with OECD identifying 241 active missions in 2025 against almost none a decade earlier, while the United Nations science, technology and innovation for Sustainable Development Goals programme supported 15 countries in developing science, technology and innovation for Sustainable Development Goals road maps between 2019 and 2025. Innovation activity, however, remains geographically concentrated: Asia accounted for around 70 per cent of patent filings in 2024, while Africa and Latin America together represented 2 per cent. Global research and development expenditure nearly tripled to $2.68 trillion between 2000 and 2022, yet 55 per cent of countries, most in the developing world, invested less than 1 per cent of GDP in research and development. Persistent skills gaps reinforce digital divides, with only 4 per cent of the population in low-income countries possessing basic digital skills against 66 per cent in high - income countries.20

Artificial intelligence innovation and investment have accelerated sharply but are highly concentrated, deepening the risk of an artificial intelligence divide. Global venture capital investment in artificial intelligence firms rose from about $8.4 billion in 2012 to $258.7 billion in 2025, with the United States accounting for three quarters of the latest-year total.21 Public policy readiness is advancing in parallel: the first session of the United Nations Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance, held in July 2026, addressed the development implications of artificial intelligence, the artificial intelligence divide, international cooperation and human oversight. The preliminary report of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence identifies insufficient scientific evidence as a crucial challenge, urging stronger country capacity to act on evidence of artificial intelligence impacts.

International cooperation, connectivity and digital finance show progress alongside persistent gaps. Scientific collaboration has lost momentum since 2019, while 74 per cent of the global population was online in 2025, yet only 23 per cent in low-income countries, against a digital infrastructure financing gap of $1.5 trillion to $1.7 trillion through 2030. Under the Sevilla Platform for Action, the International Telecommunication Union and United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and eight multilateral development banks, launched the Digital Infrastructure Investment Catalyser to close this gap. Digital financial services are expanding rapidly: mobile money use among adults in developing countries rose from 3 per cent a decade ago to 32 per cent in 2024, and global financial technology (fintech) investment rebounded to $116 billion in 2025, up from a seven -year low of $95.5 billion in 2024. However, growing spillovers from fintech, including stablecoins, potentially reaching $2 trillion by 2028, pose financial stability risks.22 Data, monitoring and follow-up

Timely, reliable, high-quality and disaggregated data and statistics are essential for advancing the financing for development agenda, which was recognized in the Sevilla Commitment. It commits to supporting developing countries in enhancing investment in data and statistical systems and to strengthen the interoperability of data and statistical frameworks for sustainable development. The Sevilla Commitment also takes important steps to strengthen the follow -up to the Financing for Development outcomes, at the national, regional and global levels. Notable progress demonstrated by strengthened data systems and infrastru cture, expanded Sustainable Development Goal indicator coverage and advances in South -South cooperation reporting is threatened by declining external financing, especially in low - income countries.

The availability and quality of data for monitoring the Sustainable Development Goals have improved substantially. Nearly 70 per cent of indicators have good coverage and all 234 indicators have well-established methodologies to date. The Global Sustainable Development Goal Indicators Database expanded to 3.3 million data records by October 2025, up from 1.4 million in 2020. 23 Nonetheless, gaps persist in disaggregated data, especially on cross-cutting dimensions, such as gender, disability and income.

Despite low global progress in statistical performance, many lower-income countries improved due to strengthened data infrastructure. However, declining external financing from 2024 onward poses a significant risk. The fall in ODA is likely to affect funding for data and statistics, which generally follows overall ODA funding trends, disproportionately affecting low-income countries. Major international programmes that support household level data collection in developing countries have experienced cuts in their funding. Notably, the abrupt termination of substantial funding for the Demographic and Health Surveys could severally impact health and gender data infrastructure in developing countries. The Financing for Development and the Future of Data, a Sevilla Platform for Action initiative, is advancing efficient data financing, future-proofing data investment and strengthening political commitment and cross‑sector coordination.

Integrated data systems and open platforms enhance accessibility and use of data and information by decision makers across sectors. The coordinated development of the System of National Accounts 2025 and Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (seventh edition) demonstrates the benefits of strategic coordinated approaches to developing modern, coherent and efficient international standards.

Progress has been achieved in South-South cooperation data reporting. In 2026, nine pilot countries in Latin American and the Caribbean reported initial data using the United Nations framework to measure South-South cooperation. Scholarships and humanitarian assistance are the leading modalities, followed by monetary contributions to infrastructure projects and technical cooperation. Complementary initiatives can play a vital role in expanding these efforts. The South -South Data Fund, created in 2025, aims to support countries to measure and report on their South- South cooperation flows. As at March 2026, 66 developing economies have requested immediate support. A community of practice to leverage South -South data, a Sevilla Platform for Action initiative, also provides a platform for peer support and technical sharing among countries.

The work to develop a framework of measures beyond GDP is progressing. The Secretary-General’s independent High-level Expert Group on Beyond GDP presented its final report on 7 May 2026, with concrete recommendations, including a conceptual framework; an indicator dashboard; and recommendations on how to implement this agenda. As a next step, Member States will initiate an intergovernmental progress to consider the recommendations of the Expert Group. This will include considering the use of the beyond GDP framework in financing policy frameworks, e.g. allocation rules for concessional finance.

The Sevilla Commitment encourages the appointment of national focal points for financing for development in finance and other relevant ministries, while General Assembly resolution 80/129 invited the Secretariat to facilitate the establishment of a network of voluntary national focal points for financing for development. After a call for nominations, the Network of National Focal Points on Financing for Development was officially launched at a high-level event in April. National focal points convened for three dedicated sessions to operationalize the network, defining possible working modalities and translating its core objectives – peer-to-peer learning and bridging national action with global financing for development commitments – into practical implementation plans. As of June 2026, the Secretariat had received nominations of 169 individuals from 87 Member States to serve as national focal points. Almost 100 of the individuals are from finance ministries. A survey of focal points conducted in May and June will inform plans for engagements and briefings during the eighty-first session of the General Assembly. National focal points will reconvene in a hybrid format at the 2027 financing for development forum.

The 2026 ECOSOC forum on financing for development follow -up, held from 20 to 24 April 2026, marked the first major intergovernmental stocktaking of progress in implementing the Sevilla Commitment. It reviewed advances and gaps across all seven action areas and highlighted priorities for implementation. The Forum also helped operationalize the strengthened follow-up architecture agreed in Sevilla, with in-depth reviews of domestic and international private business and finance; international trade as an engine for development; international financial architecture and systemic issues; and data, monitoring and follow-up and separate special high- level meetings with the Bretton Woods institutions and with the World Trade Organization and UNCTAD. The Forum’s intergovernmentally agreed outcome (E/FFDF/2026/3), adopted by consensus, sent a positive signal for multilateral cooperation at a challenging moment, recorded actions already under way and provided guidance on areas where near-term action should be concentrated.

Implementation efforts are proceeding across all action areas of the Financing for Development outcomes. In several areas, initiatives of the Sevilla Platform for Action contribute to implementation momentum and tangible progress. But the overall picture is concerning. Major aspects of international financial architecture reform, in particular those related to governance, are stalled, in a geopolitically fraught environment. In some critical areas, not least the provision of concessional financing and ODA, there is dramatic regression. The global macroeconomic and geopolitical environment remains extraordinarily challenging, exacerbating a financing squeeze for the poorest and most vulnerable countries.

In light of the holistic nature of the financing for development agenda, these setbacks threaten to undermine progress across all action areas. Full and timely implementation of the Sevilla Commitment thus remains critical. The most recent global shock underlines the need to strengthen investment in resilience and capacity for crisis response in particular.

Countries should undertake steps to sustainably mobilize resources domestically and developed countries should make every effort to not only protect support to developing countries to strengthen domestic revenue mobilization from cuts, but to scale it up to collectively at least double it by 2030, in line with the Sevilla Commitment. All countries should continue efforts to better align their fiscal systems with sustainable development; for example, the current disruptions to energy supplies underline the value of windfall taxes that can help make fiscal systems more resilient against shocks.

Rising volatility in global markets and the uneven recovery in international financing flows have also underlined the importance of countries building robust and resilient domestic financial systems. Countries should prioritize the building of a strong domestic savings base and a resilient domestic banking system that is geared towards mobilizing local savings and unlocking investment in the local economy. International support and measures to increase the availability of financing in local currency can have a catalytic effect for building and deepening domestic financial markets.

By expanding their lending during crises, multilateral development banks make important contributions to the core layers of the global financial safety net. They are demonstrating this ability in the current crisis and should consider further scaling up pre-arranged financing modalities to facilitate timely support. At the same time, the multilateral development banks and their shareholders should also develop concrete road maps towards fulfilling the ambition of the Sevilla Commitment to potentially triple their lending capacity.

Sovereign debt challenges remain a major stumbling block to financing the Sustainable Development Goal investments at scale. The progress on mainstreaming debt pause clauses in official and commercial lending is welcome; stakeholders should pursue scalable and standardized approaches, with broad triggers capable of responding to a wide range of shocks, such as those recently proposed by the London Coalition on Sustainable Sovereign Debt. At the same time, high debt service burdens continue to greatly constrain fiscal space, underlining the need for scaling up support in this area, e.g. by operationalizing the support on debt and liquidity management envisaged in the Sevilla Commitment. Complex and slow restructuring processes may have contributed to some highly indebted countries engaging in complex and sometimes opaque transactions that will further test the restructuring architecture. Member States should create and make use of inclusive spaces, such as the dialogue on debt mandated in the Sevilla Commitment, to identify gaps and proposals for closing gaps in the debt architecture.

Efforts are also needed to make the global financial safety net more responsive to shocks and emerging risks, with greater emphasis on early action, predictability, flexibility and effective coordination across institutions. The global financial safety net should be capable not only of mobilizing resources at scale, but also of delivering support rapidly, predictably, and coherently. Financing mechanisms should increasingly rely on pre-arranged instruments, including insurance and contingency financing, that can be activated rapidly when crises materialize. Early warning systems, real-time data and advanced forecasting tools can help identify risks before they escalate, allowing institutions to disburse emergency funding more quickly and effectively.

Report of the Secretary-General
Summary
The present report has been prepared pursuant to the request of the General
Assembly in its resolution 80/137 on disaster risk reduction. It provides an overview
of progress towards the goal, global targets and priorities for action of the Sendai
Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030. The report includes a section on
the implementation of the United Nations action plan to ensure that every person on
Earth is protected by early warning systems by 2027 (the Early Warnings for All
initiative) and an overview of the global response to address the impacts of the
El Niño phenomenon.
