paragraphs.text: The present report is submitted pursuant to Security Council resolution 2220 (2015), by which the Council requested the Secretary-General to continue to submit to it, on a biennial basis, a report on small arms and light weapons, including on the implementation of the resolution, as well as resolution 2616 (2021), by which the Council requested the Secretary-General to include further information on general trends of illicit trafficking and diversion in contravention of Council -mandated arms embargoes.

The report provides an overview of global, regional and subregional developments related to small arms and light weapons and of relevant actions taken by the Security Council, the United Nations, Member States and partners and includes recommendations for further action.

Since the previous report, the proliferation, misuse and diversion of small arms and light weapons have remained drivers of armed violence and have caused regional insecurity, terrorism and crime to escalate in various countries, including Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Libya, Somalia, South Sudan, the Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic and Yemen. Risks of diversion from authorized to non-authorized users persisted throughout all stages of the life cycle of these weapons, often facilitated by cross-border trafficking networks, weak border control, poor stockpile management or a lack of effective measures to regulate transfers. Furthermore, illicitly manufactured, craft-produced and 3D-printed small arms were increasingly present in global illicit markets, reflecting a growing threat to public safety.1 Meanwhile, in newly published research, it was found that an average of 88 per cent of documented incidents of conflict-related sexual violence between 2022 and 2024 involved firearms.2

The misuse of small arms and light weapons and ammunition continued to have far-reaching societal impacts. Global military spending has increased every year for a decade, reaching an all-time high of $2.7 trillion in 2024, 37 per cent higher than in 2015, when Security Council resolution 2220 (2015) was adopted, while arms production has increased in response to ongoing conflicts and geopolitical tensions. 3

The adoption of the Pact for the Future reaffirmed the commitment of Member States to addressing the risks associated with illicit small arms and light weapons within broader prevention strategies.4 The Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) declared crime and violence a public health issue, and at the fourth United Nations Conference to Review Progress Made in the Implementation of the Programme of Action to Prevent, Combat and Eradicat e the Illicit Trade in Small Arms and Light Weapons in All Its Aspects, in 2024, States Members of the United Nations reaffirmed the need to assess the linkages between armed violence associated with illicit small arms and light weapons and the health of women, men, girls and boys, which constitutes both a public health and a mental health concern, and to provide comprehensive social safety nets for victims and survivors.5 The Economic and Social Council addressed small arms and light weapons as a development issue for the first time in 2025, with the Presidents of the General Assembly and of the Economic and Social Council noting the human and economic toll of violence linked to small arms and light weapons.6 Separately, the adoption of the Global Framework for Through-life Conventional Ammunition Management in December 2023 closed a gap in the international community’s efforts to address the risks posed by conventional ammunition.

The Security Council continued to address small arms and light weapons through arms embargoes; peace operation mandates; disarmament, demobilization and reintegration programming; and thematic discussions. The Council lifted or adjusted arms embargoes in three countries,7 and technical benchmark assessments on weapons and ammunition management were carried out in four countries. 8 Violations of embargoes and illicit transfers were reported by panels of experts.

The Pact for the Future, adopted in 2024, reaffirms the centrality of small arms and light weapons control and ammunition management to building peace. As pathways for implementation, the Secretary-General recalls the recommendations outlined in his policy brief entitled “A New Agenda for Peace”.9 Member States are encouraged to set national and regional targets to combat illicit small arms and light weapons and ammunition and to pursue whole-of-government approaches that integrate small arms and light weapons control into development and violence reduction initiatives.

To integrate arms control into prevention efforts, the Secretary-General further encourages Member States to strengthen national capacities for collecting, analysing and sharing arms and ammunition flows data as part of their conflict prevention and early warning strategies. This includes investing in interoperable data systems, adopting standardized indicators and fostering collaboration between disarmament, law enforcement and early warning institutions. Experts and Member States can utilize tools such as the Arms Flows and Early Warning Dashboard, which maps existing arms flow data sets and early warning initiatives as a working tool to foster cross-thematic knowledge exchange and conduct predictive analysis.10

Separately, in response to concerns over growing military expenditure, the Secretary-General launched the report entitled “The security we need: rebalancing military spending for a sustainable and peaceful future” in September 2025.11 The Secretary-General reiterates his call upon States to advance a human-centred, multidimensional approach to security and to match any increased investments in arms with resources to through-life conventional weapons and ammunition management in order to lower the risks of diversion. 2. Sustainable development and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

Sustainable Development Goal target 16.4 contains a call to significantly reduce illicit financial and arms flows, strengthen the recovery and return of stolen assets and combat all forms of organized crime by 2030, which have yet to be achieved. Global estimates indicate that fewer than half of seized firearms are successfully traced back to their origin.12

In 2025, the Presidents of the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council convened a joint high-level meeting on small arms and light weapons. States emphasized the need for cross-sectoral approaches that serve to align arms control with national development strategies, including through strengthened national coordination, gender-responsive disarmament policies and improved data collection. To further integrate small arms and light weapons control into broader socioeconomic themes, the Secretary-General encourages enhanced cooperation between the First and Second Committees of the General Assembly.13

To integrate small arms and light weapons control and armed violence prevention into development planning, the Saving Lives Entity (SALIENT) initiative, 14 a joint programme of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Office for Disarmament Affairs, assisted eight countries, in coordination with resident coordinator offices and United Nations country teams. In 2025, the second phase, entitled SALIENT 2.0, was launched. The phase requires sustained financing from Member States in order to become operational.

Small arms and light weapons are used in both conflict and non-conflict settings. In 2024, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded at least 48,384 conflict-related deaths of civilians and persons of undetermined status, a 40 per cent increase from the previous year.15 In 2023 and 2024 combined, the main cause of death could be established for 35 per cent of cases. Of those, small arms and light weapons accounted for 6 per cent, with significant regional differences. In sub-Saharan Africa, small arms and light weapons were recorded as the cause of up to 3,243 deaths, accounting for 30 per cent of all deaths. 16

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights noted that the use of firearms contributed to high rates of violence and insecurity in society, which tend ed to affect those who were already the most disadvantaged and groups targeted on the basis of race, ethnicity, religion, and sexual orientation or gender identity. 17 The negative human rights impacts of arms transfers were examined in a n OHCHR report with a focus on public access to information on arms transfers and measures to enhance transparency.18 In the report, the Office concluded that information made available by States was often insufficient to effectively prevent, and ensure accountability for, the negative human rights impacts associated with arms transfers. The Secretary-General recommends that Member States take measures to collect and record comprehensive disaggregated data on firearms violence to facilitate evidence-based and tailored measures to protect against and prevent firearms violence.

In 2025, OHCHR identified salient gaps in the role of States and the private sector to prevent and mitigate the negative human rights impact of arms transfers. 19 The issues include high degrees of influence exercised by the arms industry over public decision-making; gaps in safeguards against prohibited transfers, including exemptions from risk assessments; insufficient efforts by States to ensure that arms manufacturers implement human rights and humanitarian law due diligence measures in arms exports; insufficient State control over transit and trans-shipment of arms; and barriers to accessing justice in relation to decisions on arms exports, including limited transparency.

Enhanced cooperation between arms control and human rights actors remains essential to mitigate the human cost of small arms and light weapons and uphold international peace and security. The Secretary-General urges Member States to implement, as appropriate, the recommendations of OHCHR for effective prevention and mitigation and to address the negative human rights impacts of arms transfers, including by strengthening oversight and transparency in arms transfer decisions and providing effective remedies for victims of violations and abuses caused or contributed to by arms, including the transfer of arms.

During the reporting period, violence against children in armed conflict increased, with a surge in the number of grave violations in comparison with 2023. 20 Small arms and light weapons affected children in armed conflicts in various ways, including through killing and maiming, recruitment and use in combat and abduction. The latest reports on children and armed conflict document the killing or injury of children by crossfire in Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti, Iraq, Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Libya, Myanmar, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Sudan and Yemen.21

A comprehensive response to end violence against children in armed conflict requires all parties to conflict to end and prevent the recruitment and use of children, cease attacks on schools and hospitals and release all children from their ranks. The Security Council is encouraged to address the role of small arms and light weapons in grave violations against children in its resolutions and deliberations, including through the Working Group on Children and Armed Conflict.

In armed conflicts, the presence of combatants carrying small arms and light weapons created an environment in which gender-based and sexual violence could occur. New research found that, in contexts where United Nations peace operations are mandated to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence, such as the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and South Sudan, an average of 88 per cent of documented conflict-related sexual violence incidents between 2022 and 2024 involved firearms. 22 The Secretary-General emphasizes the need for the systematic collection and analysis of data on the use of weapons in conflict-related sexual violence incidents, including through monitoring, analysis and reporting arrangements and other mission-level mechanisms, disaggregated by sex and age.

The vast majority of weapon-related incidents are perpetrated by men, who also represent the majority of victims of homicide and conflict-related deaths. 23 Conversely, women are overrepresented among victims of homicide committed by intimate partners or other family members.24 In this context, the Secretary-General also urges States to take measures to address cultural and social conceptions of masculinity which contribute to the perpetuation of armed violence. That also requires engaging men and boys in gender mainstreaming efforts, transforming harmful norms and promoting inclusive approaches to arms control.

Across the United Nations system, entities have advanced gender-responsive arms control. The United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa convened strategic workshops with the African Union and regional organizations to support gender mainstreaming in small arms and light weapons control, while the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific facilitated regional dialogue in Asia on integrating the women and peace and security agenda into arms control. The United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean supported national authorities in Latin America in integrating gender perspectives into firearms investigations. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) developed a global study and training module on gender dimensions of criminal justice responses to firearms-related crime, while the South Eastern and Eastern Europe Clearinghouse for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons of UNDP launched guidelines on assessing firearms risks in domestic violence and gender-responsive firearms licensing. In the area of technical ammunition management, the Women Managing Ammunition Network, now comprising 60 women experts from 43 countries, and the WoMA+ initiative have strengthened women’s participation. States are encouraged to provide targeted programmes to advance women’s equal participation in arms control and weapons and ammunition management, including in technical roles.

Young people are disproportionately affected by armed violence linked to the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, representing 37 per cent of the victims of homicides globally each year. 25 The Secretary-General encourages further research and analysis of youth-specific impacts of the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons.

Strengthening the link between the youth, peace and security agenda and arms control is essential to addressing root causes of armed violence and building sustainable peace. Youth perspectives can be integrated into national action plans, community-based violence reduction strategies and awareness-raising initiatives. Engagement with youth-led networks and civil society organizations is critical to ensuring inclusive and locally anchored approaches. Platforms such as the #Youth4Disarmament programme of the Office for Disarmament Affairs offer a valuable model for meaningful youth engagement in arms control and disarmament through dialogue, education and advocacy. The Secretary-General encourages the Security Council to promote the inclusion and participation of young people in all matters relating to their protection and support, including in arms control and disarmament forums.

Small arms and light weapons are the second most prevalent weapons used in terrorist attacks around the globe, following explosive devices. 26 In the Sahel region, small arms were used in 70 per cent of terrorist attacks.27 In the Middle East and North Africa region, the use of small arms in terrorist attacks has increased. Addressing the terrorism-arms-crime nexus, in line with Security Council resolution 2617 (2021) and previous resolutions, and disrupting the supply of weapons to terrorists require a range of measures, including border security and management strategies, enhanced stockpile management, the collection and analysis of data on the illicit trafficking of such weapons to terrorists, and the detection and disruption of criminal networks. In 2023, the General Assembly adopted resolution 77/298 on the eighth review of the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, reaffirming that Member States should prevent, combat and eradicate their illicit trade and their diversion to terrorists. Member States were called upon to find ways of intensifying and accelerating the exchange of information regarding trafficking in arms, at all levels.

To further preventing terrorist access to small arms and light weapons, the Working Group on Border Management and Law Enforcement relating to Counter - Terrorism under the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact has supported information exchange between Member States and international organizations, including on capacity-building, awareness-raising initiatives, publications and the technical guidelines to assist Member States in implementing Security Council resolution 2370 (2017). 28 The guidelines can support States in enhancing prevention and response measures to counter the acquisition and use of small arms and light weapons and ammunition. 29 The United Nations Counter- Terrorism Centre implemented several projects for building capacity to eliminate the supply of weapons to terrorists, including a project in 16 African countries, as well as providing joint support with UNODC to Central Asian countries through an inter-agency project on the terrorism-arms-crime nexus.

In assessments conducted on behalf of the Counter-Terrorism Committee, the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate continues to identify gaps in national legal and regulatory frameworks on small arms and light weapons control, such as insufficient marking and tracing systems and capacities, failure to criminalize illicit manufacturing and trafficking, and the alteration or obliteration of weapon markings. Increasingly, the Directorate has identified the manufacture of 3D -printed small arms and light weapons, parts and components by terrorists as an emerging issue. The Secretary-General calls upon Member States to strengthen efforts to implement Security Council resolution 2370 (2017), including aligning national legislation and keeping pace with emerging trends and developments related to terrorists’ acquisition of weapons.

In conflict-affected regions, such as the central Sahel, small arms and light weapons are used by terrorists and other non-State armed groups. 30 Analysis by Conflict Armament Research of the stockpiles of four armed groups in the Sahel designated by the Security Council as terrorist organizations showed that at least one fifth of recovered weapons had been diverted from State custody in North and West Africa.31

The illicit trafficking and diversion of small arms and light weapons are intertwined with organized crime, including drug trafficking, gang violence, illegal mining, the exploitation of natural resources and human smuggling. These dynamics perpetuated violence and weakened the rule of law. Transnational gangs and local criminal networks often rely on firearms to assert territorial control, enforce criminal activity and challenge State authority. Porous borders, weak regulatory frameworks and limited law enforcement capacity in Latin America and the Caribbean further facilitate the flow of weapons, many of which are trafficked between neighbouring States or diverted from national stockpiles. In post-conflict and fragile settings, the continued circulation of small arms and light weapons contributes to a “criminalized peace”, in which violence persists outside formal conflict, undermining peacebuilding and the rule of law. To address this, UNODC has supported the establishment of joint investigative teams and contact groups in Africa and Latin America, enabling transnational investigations against trafficking networks.

In Haiti, criminal groups have expanded their territorial control. The groups are equipped with firearms, many of which are trafficked from abroad and diverted from private or commercial sources. Most firearms used by the criminal groups are sourced from the United States of America or stolen and diverted from the Haitian National Police, the Haitian Armed Forces or private security companies and civilians. 32 In the absence of effective oversight, weapons intended for protective use have been redirected to criminal networks, exacerbating violence. 33 Despite the joint effort by the Haitian National Police and the General Customs Administration to reinforce public security institutions, the country’s borders remain vulnerable to the trafficking of arms and ammunition. Maritime security in Haiti has also deteriorated as criminal groups have expanded their operations to the sea, using boats to transfer arms and weapons.34

Transnational criminal dynamics were observed in Afghanistan, where possible arms and ammunition transfer to neighbouring States in breach of the arms embargo and unofficial markets for weapons have emerged, further escalating the threat to regional security.35 Arms seizures were made in several countries, including Pakistan and Tajikistan, with the origin of the arms traced to Afghanistan. In response, a weapons registration and monitoring commission was initiated by the de facto authorities to implement an arms licensing and stockpile management system, as well as to seize weapons caches from individual commanders.

In West Africa, UNODC supported law enforcement operations with code names such as KAFO IV and KAFO V that led to seizures of firearms and ammunition.36 The International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL) led intelligence operations resulting in arms and ammunition seizures in Latin America, the Caribbean and South- East Asia. In the Western Balkans, 4,984 firearms were seized inland and at the borders in 2024, and the South Eastern and Eastern Europe Clearinghouse for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons supported the development of standard operating procedures for detection and investigations, and the provision of equipment. In the Caribbean, the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean continued to conduct national training for detecting arms, ammunition and components using X-ray technology.

States are encouraged to adopt integrated criminal justice responses, including legal frameworks, that support investigations and prosecutions of the small arms and light weapons trafficking offences while aiming to reveal and dismantle organized crime groups and networks and their possible nexus with other forms of crime. States are also encouraged to systematically collect and analyse disaggregated data on illicitly trafficked small arms and light weapons and their criminal context in order to identify trends and patterns.

The targeted integration of weapons and ammunition management considerations into Security Council mandates remains essential in broader peace and security, sanction regimes and peacebuilding processes. In 2025, the third edition of the aide-memoire on options for reflecting weapons and ammunition management in decisions of the Security Council was published with a dashboard that includes a catalogue of good practice language. 37 The Secretary-General encourages the Security Council to consider weapons and ammunition management in relevant resolutions and make use of the aide-memoire.

In line with Security Council resolution 2117 (2013), United Nations peacekeeping operations are well placed to support weapons and ammunition management and, in particular, to monitor illicit arms flows and initiate the tracing of recovered materiel to enable national authorities to open investigations on the matter. Since the previous report on small arms and light weapons, the Council has reinforced its commitment to weapons and ammunition management through resolutions renewing peace operation mandates. In its resolutions 2755 (2024) on Libya, 2759 (2024) on the Central African Republic and 2765 (2024) on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Council explicitly mandated United Nations missions to support national authorities in securing stockpiles, clearing explosive remnants of war and preventing diversion. In Haiti, the Multinational Security Support Mission was transitioned to the Gang Suppression Force and authorized to provide support to the Haitian National Police and the Haitian Armed Forces to combat illicit trafficking and the diversion of arms and related materiel, including to seize and collect, record , and dispose of illicit arms and ammunition.38

The drawdown and closure of peace operations present challenges for assistance to strengthen weapons and ammunition management. Many mandates of United Nations peacekeeping operations currently include provisions to support weapons and ammunition management. 39 To ensure that gains in weapons and ammunition management are not reversed, it is critical to avoid operational gaps, support a smooth post-mission transition and mitigate the risk of the renewed illicit circulation of weapons and ammunition.

To strengthen the safe and secure management of deployed weapons and ammunition in peace operations, the United Nations launched specialized training material on weapons and ammunition management in peace operations to enhance the capacities of troop- and police-contributing countries. 40 The Secretary-General encourages Member States responsible for delivering training to units designated for United Nations peace operations to incorporate the material into training programmes.

In operational settings, the Mine Action Service provided tailored support for weapons and ammunition management, ranging from technical training to policy support, marking and destruction. In Somalia, a central monitoring department was established under the Office of National Security, serving as an example of how early measures can support the easing of the transition period ahead of changes to arms embargoes. In Abyei, the Mine Action Service component of the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei facilitated the destruction of illicit small arms and light weapons and ammunition. In South Sudan, technical assistance to troop - and police-contributing countries enabled the safe disposal of close to 1 million rounds of unserviceable small arms ammunition. In the Central African Republic, the Mine Action Service component of the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) delivered training sessions for the Armed Forces of the Central African Republic, the Internal Security Forces and MINUSCA, reaching 396 personnel, including the first -ever weapons and ammunition management training of trainers. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the progressive withdrawal of United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo forces required measures to prevent the diversion of surplus weapons and ammunition, the Mine Action Service component of the Mission supported the safe destruction of almost 1.4 million rounds of small arms ammunition. Furthermore, in the aftermath of the fall of Goma in January 2025, more than 2,000 weapons, nearly 7,000 weapons components and over 54,000 rounds of small arms ammunition were surrendered to the Mission and destroyed. The Secretary-General encourages the Security Council, when establishing the mandates of United Nations peacekeeping operations and special political missions, to include arms expertise within their structures and enhance cooperation with other relevant United Nations entities to strengthen the collection, analysis and use of arms flow data.

United Nations entities and regional partners, in cooperation with the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR), continued to use the Institute’s reference methodology to conduct assessments at the request of States, including in countries and situations under the purview of the Security Council such as the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Somalia, as well as West African States not under the purview of the Council. 41 Furthermore, UNIDIR and the Office for Disarmament Affairs developed the Modular Small-arms- control Implementation Compendium assessment tool to support Member States in assessing their national small arms control systems in operational areas. Assessments were conducted by the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific and the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa, in Burundi, Cambodia, the Gambia, Fiji and Nepal.

In the Caribbean, the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean assisted national authorities with weapons marking, physical security and stockpile management and the disposal of weapons in Barbados, the Dominican Republic, Grenada, Jamaica and Saint Kitts and Nevis. Over 360 firearms and 12,500 rounds of ammunition were destroyed. The Regional Centre published a policy framework on the sustainable disposal of destroyed firearms and ammunition components, developed with the CARICOM Implementation Agency for Crime and Security and the Mines Advisory Group. 42 In South-East Europe, the South Eastern and Eastern Europe Clearinghouse for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons made advances in the physical security and stockpile management of small arms and light weapons and ammunition, which included the destruction of more than 2,000 weapons. In 2024, national reports on the implementation of the Programme of Action on Small Arms indicated th at national authorities in 67 of 100 reporting countries had collected 860,598 weapons, of which 65 per cent were destroyed.

During the reporting period, elements of through-life weapons and ammunition management were increasingly integrated with disarmament, demobilization and reintegration processes. In Ghana, the United Nations delivered training to strengthen the capacity of disarmament, demobilization and reintegration practitioners, as well as to implement the safe handling, storage and destruction of weapons and ammunition. In Somalia, a study on weapons and ammunition dynamics in the context of disarmament, demobilization and reintegration served to emphasize the need to enhance federal-State coordination, supporting voluntary defections and promoting sustainable reintegration in newly recovered areas.43 In the Central African Republic, MINUSCA supported the Government in conducting disarmament and demobilization operations, which led to the disarmament of more than 700 combatants and the collection of over 600 weapons and over 25,000 rounds of ammunition. In South Sudan, the United Nations Mission in South Sudan supported national authorities in strengthening community violence reduction and weapons and ammunition management efforts through capacity-building, strategic planning and policy integration. The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo also strengthened the weapons and ammunition management capacity of the national Disarmament, Demobilization, Community Recovery and Stabilization Programme.

The Secretary-General reiterates his recommendation to the Security Council to continue to promote the integration of weapons and ammunition management into disarmament, demobilization and reintegration processes and community violence reduction programmes, including through dedicated mandates of peace operations. He further recommends the targeted integration of through-life weapons and ammunition management into conflict prevention, peacebuilding and sustaining peace, security sector governance and reform, and the women and peace and security agenda.

During the reporting period, persistent violations of Security Council -mandated arms embargoes were documented by panels and groups of experts, reflecting the continuing need to enhance national implementation and closer regional cooperation. Systematic embargo breaches persisted by air, maritime and overland routes, and panels documented external supply chains to armed actors and diversion from stockpiles.

ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida and affiliates continued to exploit weak State capacity to control arms and borders, procuring small arms and light weapons through transnational trafficking networks. In the Syrian Arab Republic, ISIL (Da ’esh) and Al-Qaida affiliates purchased substantial quantities of arms diverted from abandoned former government stocks. 44 ISIL (Da’esh) in Somalia smuggled small arms in coordination with (ISIL) Da’esh in Yemen to support the global operations of ISIL (Da’esh).

The Central African Republic reached a significant milestone in July 2024, when the Security Council, in its resolution 2745 (2024), lifted the comprehensive arms embargo while maintaining the targeted arms embargo against armed groups and associated individuals. Armed groups continue to procure weapons through regional trafficking networks, as documented in the report of the Panel of Experts pursuant to Security Council resolution 2745 (2024) on illicit arms transfers.45

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Group of Experts reported on persistent violations of the arms embargo, 46 including cross-border transfers and illicit military support to armed groups. In October 2023, the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1533 (2004) concerning the Democratic Republic of the Congo listed two individuals for such violations. 47

In Haiti, despite the Security Council’s decision to impose measures including a targeted arms embargo in 2022, illicit trafficking of weapons and ammunition has continued unabated, fuelling high levels of armed violence and the increasingly sophisticated weaponry in gangs’ possession.48 The sophistication and volume of the shipment suggest well-established supply chains, while border security in Haiti remained limited, facilitating the steady flow of arms.49 In October 2023, the Security Council replaced the targeted embargo with a territorial embargo and, in October 2024, further expanded its scope by prohibiting transfers of all arms and related materiel of all types, military vehicles, equipment and spare parts, as well as related technical assistance, financing and training.

The Panel of Experts on Libya established pursuant to resolution 1973 (2011) reported on ongoing violations of the arms embargo, including the acquisition of dual - use equipment by armed actors. The Panel assessed that the arms embargo remained ineffective, as armed actors obtained weapons and ammunition in areas where logistical supply chains were controlled by Member States.50

In December 2023, the Security Council lifted the general arms embargo on Somalia through resolution 2714 (2023) while imposing a general and complete arms embargo on Al-Shabaab through resolution 2713 (2023). The Panel of Experts established pursuant to resolution 2713 (2023) reported on challenges faced by Somalian authorities in safely and securely managing weapons and ammunition due to illicit weapons trafficking, lack of accountability over heavily armed clan militias, and the limited analysis and tracing capacity of seized weapons, ammunition and improvised explosive devices.51

In South Sudan, the Security Council, by its resolution 2683 (2023), decided that the notification requirements set out in paragraph 2 of resolution 2633 (2022) should no longer apply to the supply, sale or transfer of non-lethal military equipment, solely in support of the implementation of the terms of the peace agreement, and related technical assistance or training on non-lethal military equipment. However, more progress is needed in weapons and ammunition management, as concluded in the most recent benchmark assessment.52 In addition, the Panel of Experts established pursuant to Security Council resolution 2206 (2015) reported on possible violations of the arms embargo involving the procurement of military equipment and training related to military activities.53

In the Darfur region of the Sudan, arms proliferation continues to fuel conflict and the growth of arms sales in the black market across Darfur. The Rapid Support Forces have obtained sophisticated weaponry and developed decentralized supply chains, enabling the Forces to counter the air superiority of the Sudanese Armed Forces, as documented by the Panel of Experts on the Sudan established pursuant to resolution 1591 (2005).54

In Yemen, the illicit trafficking of small arms and light weapons bound for Houthi forces remained significant. Most shipments are transported across the Arabian Sea by dhows and small boats. International maritime forces intercepted multiple large consignments bound for the Houthis, seizing 750 tons of small arms and light weapons in June 2025.55 The Secretary-General urges Member States subject to arms embargoes to strengthen their national security institutions and to cooperate with panels or groups of experts, which are critical in monitoring, investigating and documenting arms embargo violations and trends. The Secretary-General further encourages States to provide timely responses to tracing requests and to share relevant information to support experts’ investigations. Benchmarks on weapons and ammunition management in the context of arms embargoes

The lifting of the arms embargoes on the Central African Republic 56 and Somalia57 and adjustments to the arms embargo provisions on South Sudan 58 by the Security Council reflect steps taken by those States to strengthen their effective arms and ammunition management. Where embargo regimes have been partially or fully lifted, greater responsibility is placed on the Government for continued attention to weapons and ammunition. Following the lifting of the arms embargo in the Central African Republic, MINUSCA, through the Mine Action Service and in collaboration with the National Commission for the Fight against the Proliferation of Small Arms and Light Weapons, supported efforts to improve weapons and ammunition management for strengthening national resilience in support of Security Council priorities.

To support reviews of arms embargoes, the Security Council established benchmarks related to weapons and ammunition management, which have proven to be valuable tools for assessing progress under relevant sanctions regimes. Such assessments were conducted in the context of the Central African Republic,59 Haiti,60 Somalia61 and South Sudan.62 Regarding Somalia, in October 2024, the Secretary- General presented a progress update to the Council on the implementation of benchmarks as set out in his letter dated 15 September 2022 addressed to the President of the Security Council. 63 An additional benchmark on the safe management of chemical precursors associated with improvised explosive devices was added to existing benchmarks on weapons and ammunition management, including on legal frameworks, coordination mechanisms, marking and record-keeping, stockpiles, verification processes, traceability of recovered weapons, combating sexual violence and implementation of the road map on children in armed conflict. 64 Member States and relevant international and regional organizations are encouraged to provide capacity-building for national authorities to exert effective arms and ammunition management.

In 2025, members of the Security Council convened an Arria -formula meeting on small arms control and weapons management in United Nations sanctions regimes, initiated by Sierra Leone and co-sponsored by Algeria, Guyana and Somalia. Member States and briefers underscored the importance of arms embargoes as entry points for strengthening weapons and ammunition management, and challenges such as weak border control, limited political will and poor stockpile management were highlighted.

At the fourth United Nations Conference to Review Progress Made in the Implementation of the Programme of Action to Prevent, Combat and Eradicate the Illicit Trade in Small Arms and Light Weapons in All Its Aspects and the International Instrument to Enable States to Identify and Trace, in a Timely and Reliable Manner, Illicit Small Arms and Light Weapons, in June 2024, States adopted, by consensus, a political declaration and action-oriented measures for the period 2024–2030. 65 Following a decade of discussion within the meetings of the Programme of Action, States agreed to establish an open-ended technical expert group tasked with developing recommendations on developments in technology, manufacturing and design in small arms and light weapons. The group is mandated to identify and examine opportunities presented by emerging technologies such as improved marking and record-keeping while also addressing challenges, in particular polymer and modular weapons and firearms produced using 3D printing. The group will convene during biennial meetings in 2026 and 2028, with final recommendations to be considered no later than 2030.

At the Conference, States emphasized the need for sustained international cooperation and assistance and agreed to establish a structured procedure to facilitate matching assistance needs and offers or implementing the Programme of Action and International Tracing Instrument. Separately, the General Assembly mandated a small arms and light weapons control fellowship aimed at strengthening national authorities’ conceptual and practical knowledge while fostering regional and global communities of practice. 66 The Office for Disarmament Affairs launched the fellowship in July 2025 with a first iteration in the Caribbean.

The Conference also marked a thematic shift towards addressing both supply - and demand-side drivers of illicit small arms and light weapons, including environmental and socioeconomic factors. Member States also strengthened commitments to gender-responsive small arms and light weapons control and the integration of youth perspectives.67

In addition, States noted that seized small arms and light weapons often had unique identifying marks, such as serial numbers, that were deliberately removed by unauthorized users to obstruct tracing efforts. To address this growing concern, a United Nations study on obliterated markings and methods for marking recovery in the context of the International Tracing Instrument is being conduct ed by the Office for Disarmament Affairs and Conflict Armament Research. 2. Global framework on through-life conventional ammunition management

The adoption of the Global Framework for Through-life Conventional Ammunition Management by the General Assembly in December 2023 through resolution 78/111 represents a significant milestone in the international community ’s efforts to address the risks posed by conventional ammunition. The Framework promotes safe, secure and sustainable ammunition management throughout the life cycle in order to prevent diversion, illicit trafficking and unplanned explosions.

At a preparatory meeting of States convened at United Nations Headquarters in June 2025 an outcome document was adopted without a vote, underscoring continued consensus on the need to address ammunition risks through a life-cycle approach encompassing production, marking, storage, transfer, use and disposal. 68 Member States established the structure, modalities and processes for an effective follow -up and review mechanism and laid the foundation for the first meeting of States in 2027.

Member States endorsed a voluntary reporting template developed by the Secretariat as well as the establishment of a biennial reporting cycle, starting in 2028, with a request for initial overviews in 2026.

The Arms Trade Treaty, with its 117 States Parties and 25 signatories, remained a key instrument for preventing the illicit trade and diversion of conventional arms and ammunition. Since November 2023, Colombia, the Gambia, Malawi and Vanuatu have joined the Treaty. States Parties have continued to demonstrate their commitment to addressing the diversion of small arms and light weapons as well as effectively implementing the Treaty’s provisions to mitigate risks.

The ninth Conference of States Parties to the Treaty, held in August 2023, was focused on the role of industry in responsible international transfers of conventional arms. States Parties were encouraged to develop a list of possible reference documents to support industry compliance with national control systems and welcomed the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights: Implementing the United Nations “Protect, Respect and Remedy” Framework. The tenth Conference of States Parties, held in August 2024, was focused on the role of interagency cooperation in effective treaty implementation, recommending the development of voluntary guidance to support States Parties on this issue. The Conference endorsed a voluntary guide, to be continuously reviewed and updated, for implementing articles 6 and 7 on prohibitions and export risk assessments which can be used by States establishing or improving their national control systems. In August 2025, States Parties held the eleventh Conference of States Parties, committed to enhancing gender mainstreaming and youth engagement efforts in their work with the Treaty and adopted a decision to establish gender focal points under the Treaty. 69 States Parties further agreed to discuss the development of voluntary guidance that links industry responsibilities under human rights and international humanitarian law with the obligations of States Parties under the Treaty.

The Diversion Information and Exchange Forum continued to be a platform for States Parties and signatory States to voluntarily exchange information on substantive cases of detected or suspected diversion and share operational diversion -related information. To date, the Forum has met six times. 70 The Secretary-General encourages States Parties and signatory States to continue to use the Forum, to foster information exchange and to facilitate international cooperation to prevent and eradicate the diversion of arms. 4. Protocol against the Illicit Manufacturing of and Trafficking in Firearms, Their Parts and Components and Ammunition, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

The Protocol against the Illicit Manufacturing of and Trafficking in Firearms, Their Parts and Components and Ammunition provided preventive measures against the illicit manufacturing of and trafficking in firearms, their parts and components, as well as criminal justice responses to such crimes. In its resolution 12/3 of 2024, 71 the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime encouraged States to strengthen the capacities of law enforcement and criminal justice authorities to detect, investigate, prosecute and adjudicate new and emerging forms of illicit manufacturing of and trafficking in firearms and to conduct risk assessments of ammunition stockpiles with a view to preventing unplanned explosions and the diversion of ammunition.

At its eleventh meeting, in April 2024, the Working Group on Firearms advanced discussion on emerging threats such as the use of postal and courier services for trafficking, 3D-printed firearm components, and the criminalization of digital blueprints.72 At the twelfth meeting of the Working Group, it was recommended that States and relevant international organizations conduct inquiries in order to address the proliferation of uncontrolled illicitly acquired leftover weapons in post -conflict situations, to identify risks of diversion to criminal organizations and terrorist groups and to prevent crimes and regional destabilization. The Working Group requested UNODC to foster its cooperation with United Nations peacekeeping and special political missions as well as United Nations resident coordinator offices to strengthen firearms-related expertise within their respective entities, including the consideration of arms-related early warning indicators in order to better support preventative action.73

In 2024 and 2025, the Group of Governmental Experts on the Register of Conventional Arms discussed the potential expansion of the scope of the Register. While consensus was not reached on the proposal for creating an eighth category of small arms and light weapons, the Group’s deliberations laid the groundwork for future consideration. The Group also discussed newly adopted international agreements and processes on conventional arms and ammunition and the implications of expanding the scope of Member State legislative and regulatory frameworks governing participation in the Register. During the 2024 cycle for reporting to the Register, 72 per cent of 68 Member States that submitted a report to the Register provided information on their transfers of small arm s and light weapons.

Member States in a position to do so are encouraged to continue to use, on a voluntary basis, the “seven-plus-one” formula and the description provided by the 2022 Group of Governmental Experts on the Register of Conventional Arms, in order to provide information on transfers of small arms and light weapons, and to continue to make efforts, where possible, to disaggregate data reported to the Register, including when reporting transfers of small arms and light weapons.74

Regional and subregional road maps have continued to evolve as strategic instruments for addressing illicit small arms and light weapons challenges in a coordinated and sustainable manner. The adoption of the Central America and Dominican Republic Road Map for Preventing the Illicit Trafficking and Proliferation of Firearms, Ammunition and Explosives in February 2025 marked a major milestone. Developed through a consultative process led by the Organization of American States and the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean, in collaboration with the Central American Integration System, the road map outlines priority actions up to 2035 and includes a performance-based monitoring framework and a pillar on the prevention of violence with firearms.75

The Western Balkans Small Arms and Light Weapons Control Road Map, adopted in 2018 and facilitated by UNDP and the South Eastern and Eastern Europe Clearinghouse for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons, continued to be a sustainable regional approach for preventing and countering the misuse, illegal possession and trafficking of firearms, ammunition and explosives. The second phase of the road map for the period 2025–2030 was endorsed at the European Union- Western Balkans Ministerial Forum on Justice and Home Affairs held in October 2024, which reconfirmed the emphasis on institutional sustainability, a whole-of- government and -society approach, gender mainstreaming and youth inclusion, effective response to threats, and alignment with European Union regulatory frameworks.76 The United Nations multi-partner trust fund, established by UNDP and UNODC, supported the implementation of the road map in the amount of approximately $28.5 million.

The Roadmap for Implementing the Caribbean Priority Actions on the Illicit Proliferation of Firearms and Ammunition across the Caribbean in a Sustainable Manner by 2030, adopted in 2020, continues to guide regional implementation for CARICOM States and is supported by the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean and the Implementation Agency for Crime and Security of CARICOM as co -custodians and by UNDP and UNODC as implementing partners. The road map is also supported by the World Customs Organization, which carried out a joint operation with the Implementation Agency in 2024 for customs administrations from across the Caribbean. The operation enhanced capabilities and operational coordination to d etect and intercept illicit small arms and light weapons, their components and ammunition, resulting in the seizure of more than 350 firearms.

In South-East Asia, the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Asia and the Pacific supported the operationalization of the Declaration on Combating Arms Smuggling adopted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations countries in August 2023 during the Association’s seventeenth Ministerial Meeting on Transnational Crime, signalling a strengthened regional commitment to arms control, enhanced border cooperation and intelligence -sharing. The support was focused on aligning strategies with the Programme of Action on Small Arms and the International Tracing Instrument, enhancing inter-agency coordination, sharing data and addressing emerging threats.

In Africa, the Silencing the Guns by 2030 initiative of the African Union continues to guide continental peace efforts, with its Peace and Security Council emphasizing the need to recalibrate conflict prevention tools and integrate socioeconomic development into peacebuilding at its 2024 session in Bangui. Meanwhile, through Africa Amnesty Month, jointly coordinated by the Office for Disarmament Affairs, the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa and the African Union, assistance was provided to the Central African Republic, Djibouti and Rwanda, with symbolic weapons destruction and public awareness campaigns reinforcing voluntary disarmament.

In 2024, the Department of Peace Operations and the Office for Disarmament Affairs, together with the Bonn International Centre for Conflict Studies, supported the Regional Centre on Small Arms in the Great Lakes Region, the Horn of Africa and Bordering States in developing the first regional road map of its kind on weapons and ammunition management in disarmament, demobilization and reintegration settings. The road map serves as a strategic instrument for enhancing small arms and light weapons control in the region by promoting regional coordination, aligned policy development, capacity-building and community engagement and includes mechanisms for monitoring and review. In July 2025, the Regional Centre and UNIDIR launched a comprehensive review of the Nairobi Protocol for the Prevention, Control and Reduction of Small Arms and Light Weapons in the Great Lakes Region and the Horn of Africa, marking its twentieth anniversary.

Furthermore, cross-regional exchanges are encouraged to promote the exchange of practices of the regional and subregional models. During the reporting period, study visits by Cambodia, Honduras and Kyrgyzstan to the Western Balkans allowed for such exchanges. States are encouraged to reinforce existing mechanisms and, where appropriate, establish new ones that reflect regional specificities and priorities with regard to illicit small arms and light weapons and through-life conventional ammunition management.

Developments in small arms and light weapons technology, manufacturing and design pose both challenges and opportunities for preventing and combating illicit small arms and light weapons. During the reporting period, States and experts expressed concern regarding illicitly craft-manufactured, converted, privately manufactured weapons and those produced through the illicit use of additive manufacturing technologies such as 3D printing. Modular weapon design and the use of polymer materials continued to complicate tracing efforts and effective arms control. In response, the Secretary-General encourages Member States to actively engage in the open-ended technical expert group to be established under the Programme of Action on Small Arms and the International Tracing Instrument, by nominating relevant experts and contributing substantive inputs in order to ensure inclusive and timely recommendations.

A global study on craft-produced weapons found that national regulatory approaches remain fragmented and that many States face difficulties in addressing the challenges posed by craft-produced or artisanal weapons, systems and components.77 Moreover, 3D-printing technologies enable the decentralized, home- based production of firearm components, with production instructions accessible on the dark web as well as on social media platforms and messenger services. 78 Some countries have taken steps to regulate the craft production of small arms and light weapons, including the regulation of prefabricated kits and digital blueprints shared online. 79 Member States are encouraged to take steps to regulate, through national legislation, digital blueprints and the electronic sharing of designs and construction data for the illicit manufacturing of firearms and components.

States Parties to the Protocol against the Illicit Manufacturing of and Trafficking in Firearms, Their Parts and Components and Ammunition have been encouraged to criminalize the illicit possession, uploading, downloading and transfer of blueprints for the 3D printing of firearms intended for illicit manufacturing and criminal use. 80 The United Nations Convention against Cybercrime; Strengthening International Cooperation for Combating Certain Crimes Committed by Means of Information and Communications Technology Systems and for the Sharing of Evidence in Electronic Form of Serious Crimes, adopted by the General Assembly in December 2024, offers a platform for international cooperation in combating cybercrime, including the illicit online trade of small arms and light weapons.81

Technologies can also positively support marking, tracing, record -keeping and identification efforts. Through research, UNIDIR and the Flemish Peace Institute developed a framework for identification and assessment of the utility and feasibility of using specific technologies in the detection, prevention and mitigation of the diversion of conventional arms. 82 The research served to identify 14 emerging technologies in this regard. Furthermore, the use of technologies such as global navigation satellite system tracking and DNA tagging has been recommended by the Working Group on Firearms under the Firearms Protocol to prevent diversion during deliveries of firearms. Separately, advances in the practical application of new technologies to conventional ammunition were made, including stamping, laser marking and chemical taggants.83 During the reporting period, Somalia became the first country in the world to adopt AmTag, a chemical taggant applied to ammunition, which renders the national stockpile fully traceable and enables investigators to audit chains of custody, identify cases of theft or corruption and deter criminal activity.84

Online tools are used to enhance tracing and investigations by law enforcement agencies. Since the previous report, the INTERPOL Firearms Reference Table has been expanded and now contains over 165,000 individual firearms references and more than 51,000 firearms entries. States are encouraged to further expand entries to support the identification of privately manufactured firearms and 3D-printed weapons. The INTERPOL Illicit Arms Records and Tracing Management System is another tool for maintaining standardized records of weapons transfers and seizures through the secure I-24/7 network. The system enhances real-time information exchange among 196 member countries, as well as with key partners such as the World Customs Organization and the European Union Agency for Law Enfor cement Cooperation. In addition, the Arms Registration and Management System is a new weapon and ammunition management system designed by Conflict Armament Research specifically for use in challenging, low infrastructure environments t o support investigations into instances of weapon diversion, which resulted in a number of prosecutions during the reporting period.

Illicit small arms and light weapons continued to pose a complex challenge to international peace and security with devastating consequences for lives, livelihoods and sustainable development across all regions. The demand for and influx of weapons and ammunition into armed conflict situations heighten the risks of the diversion of small arms and light weapons to unauthorized recipients, even years after conflicts have ended.

Preventing diversion and illicit trade requires comprehensive interventions at every stage of the life cycle of weapons – from the point of manufacture, pre-transfer, transfer, border controls, transport, retransfer, marking, tracing, record -keeping, stockpiling and recovery to their eventual use or disposal and the investigation and analysis of diversion. States are encouraged to share operationally relevant information to help prevent, detect and address diversion. To strengthen global accountability and improve the effectiveness of tracing mechanisms, it is critical to expand the number of States that regularly participate in weapons tracing efforts. States can make use of existing tools, including the INTERPOL Illicit Arms Records and Tracing Management System and the Arms Registration and Management System. Member States are encouraged to explore and share among them good practices on the use of advanced technologies to improve marking, record -keeping, tracing and stockpile management and to prevent diversion.

Given the persistence of transnational trafficking networks that exploit porous borders and maritime routes, particularly in the Sahel, West Africa and the Caribbean, and the uneven capacity of customs and border control authorities to detect and investigate illicit transfers, cross-border cooperation can be enhanced. States have previously agreed to establish or strengthen subregional and regional cooperation, including monitoring cross-border trafficking through information-sharing, as feasible. Separately, there is a lack of disaggregated data on ammunition trafficking, which continues to hinder evidence-based policymaking on ammunition management. To address this gap and improve understanding of diversion and trafficking trends, the Secretary-General encourages the Security Council to promote regional instruments, processes and regional cooperation to strengthen border security and export and import licensing systems. This could include establishing joint border task forces, using interoperable data-sharing platforms or exchanging experiences with end-user certificates. Furthermore, the Secretary-General encourages the Security Council to support regional approaches to address illicit small arms and light weapons, recognizing the importance of coordinated action by regional and subregional organizations.

Stockpile diversion remained a major source of small arms and light weapons for illicit actors including terrorist groups, particularly in conflict -affected regions. Member States are encouraged to strengthen physical security and stockpile management to prevent diversion from State and non-State custody, in conflict and fragile regions. Measures should include regular risk assessments, physical upgrades to storage sites, inventory reconciliation, personnel vetting and the timely destruction of surplus weapons, in line with the Modular Small-arms-control Implementation Compendium tool and the International Ammunition Technical Guidelines.

Comprehensive and effective weapons and ammunition management is dependent on sustained funding. While challenges related to small arms and light weapons are growing in many parts of the world, donor contributions have been declining. Diversion risks have been documented, particularly in fragile contexts and in sanctions-monitoring settings. There is an urgent need for targeted assistance to strengthen marking, tracing, and stockpile security. In line with the Security Council ’s efforts to prevent and address illicit small arms and light weapons, the Secretary- General recommends that Member States acquiring small arms and light weapons and ammunition consider ensuring sustained funding for management and control to prevent diversion. Furthermore, donors are encouraged to provide financing aligned with national priorities and coordinated through relevant United Nations and regional mechanisms to ensure sustained capacity and accountability.
